production read/child/snapshot/output adapters, peer-binding refresh across
reporter changes, authoritative permanent-loss handling and real distributed
restart proof remain outstanding. The broader scheduler gaps listed above also
remain open. Full qualification remains waived and the full design is unfinished.


### Permanent remote initialization authority (2026-10-14)

Metadata now stores a permanent first-use grant for each enrolled physical root,
independently of administrative retirement enrollment. Root-signed preparation
reserves an immutable initialization ID; activation advances that same ID and
cannot be downgraded by delayed preparation. Both preflight and Raft apply check
the metadata realm, registered root/key and current reporter. Store removal and
re-registration retain the grant, as do metadata restart and snapshot restore.
The new transition requires coordinated decoder version 34 before proposal.

Preparation, activation and signed status use the existing internal catalog route
without setting-administrator authority. The handler requires a host-verified
service token even in migration mode; root signatures provide store authority.
Uncertain commit outcomes remain uncertain and can be resolved through status.
Six targeted tests pass, with no leaks, across 51 build steps. Source and binary
evidence is recorded in `remote-initialization-grant-main-2c8240-oct14-application.json`.

This completes the metadata grant mechanism only. Journal ID binding, locked
first-use validation, durable publication history, activation before exposing
control ingress and automatic node initialization still need implementation.
External-work recovery and production remote reads remain closed. The full
design remains unfinished; full qualification remains waived.


### Journal initialization binding and publication history (2026-10-14)

The private journal now uses format v3 (same basename), persisting its metadata
initialization ID and a sticky publication flag. `openAuthorized` obtains fresh
authority only after acquiring the exclusive journal lock. Prepared grants permit
creation or retry of an unused matching checkpoint; active grants only permit
reopening that exact checkpoint. Missing active, mismatched, unbound and legacy
journals fail closed. No automatic legacy migration or replacement is performed.

Inbound worker admission persists the publication flag before gate admission or
physical ownership. Outbound dispatch persists it with destination history before
wire publication. File/directory sync failures prevent admission and poison the
owner until reopen. Epoch changes and terminal outcomes never clear the flag;
load rejects an unused flag combined with published destination history.
The scoped read-admission helper carries the existing CPU wait boundary through
journal I/O. The TCP read fixture retains its query root while lending CPU during
the first journal sync; its original cancellation and deadline checks remain.

All 46 component tests pass (the final identical component target is cached).
The unchanged final API binary passes all 16 tests with localhost access, with no
leaks. The sandbox run passed 14 and failed the two TCP fixtures; its earlier
localhost rerun exposed an unscoped fixture sync, now corrected and verified.
Evidence is pinned in `remote-journal-initialization-binding-main-2c8240-oct14-application.json`.

The API bootstrap still uses the explicit low-level open/create path; it has not
yet been switched to this metadata-authorized opener. Automatic node first use,
metadata activation before exposing ingress, and unused-journal recovery proof
consumption are next. Production remote reads and prior external-work recovery
remain closed. The full design remains unfinished; full qualification is waived.


### Automatic metadata-authorized node bootstrap (2026-10-14)

The node control round now permits first use without a pre-existing journal.
The API loads the physical root signing identity, resolves the registered local
and destination keys, and opens the journal through `openAuthorized`. While the
journal lock is held, a signed linearizable status reads existing authority; only
missing authority proceeds to coordinated preparation. A random candidate never
replaces an existing ID. All metadata calls retain the original bootstrap budget.

The owner constructs durable state and bounded transports, then activates the
exact journal ID in metadata before starting reconciliation or exposing control
ingress. A lost activation response requires a fresh matching active status;
blocked/ambiguous activation destroys unpublished state and leaves retryable
prepared journal state. Caller-selected open/initialize mode was removed from the
bootstrap descriptor; API ABI v32 rejects older layouts before reading them.

Only a matching, active journal whose sticky flag proves no work was ever
published can complete recovery automatically. The recovery callback reads that
durable evidence under the journal mutex while ingress is still unpublished.
Once publication is recorded, later processes remain closed pending genuine
external-work recovery. Missing active journals, old/unbound state and mismatched
root enrollment remain fail-closed. Production owned reads are still disabled.

Ten metadata/handshake/journal tests, two direct/opaque owner and transport
allocation tests, 16 API/TCP tests and the ABI-prefix test pass without leaks.
The component target is cached (46 tests previously passed). The actual non-test
node/opaque bridge passes semantic analysis in 45 build steps; this is not a live
cluster restart test. The owner and API binaries pass unchanged with localhost
access after their sandbox-blocked TCP fixtures. Source/binary receipts are in
`remote-authorized-bootstrap-main-2c8240-oct14-application.json`.

Remaining work includes recovery after published external work, production
read/child/snapshot/output ownership adapters, peer binding refresh, permanent
loss handling, distributed overload/restart proof and the broader scheduler gaps
listed above. The full design remains unfinished; full qualification is waived.


### Physical parent retention across remote uncertainty (2026-10-14)

The fixed coordinator outbox now accepts a move-only physical parent reference
before wire publication. The worker lease adapter obtains an additional resource
reference; no per-child reconciliation allocation is introduced. Retained client
dispatch transfers the reference into the reserved slot. Failure before transfer
leaves ownership with the caller; unpublished rollback after transfer releases it.
A published response, timeout, cancellation request, abandonment or new epoch
does not release the parent. Signed terminal/fence reconciliation retires only
the matching attempt/destination.

Retirement marks the slot before calling its parent release callback outside the
ledger mutex. The slot, attempt count and byte charge remain occupied throughout
the callback, preventing capacity reuse before physical release. Reentrant status,
duplicate terminal calls and late transport completion cannot release twice or
revive retirement. API owner destruction rejects remaining parent references
rather than dropping them with uncertain ledger state. Retention contexts must
remain stable until release and must not borrow a returning request's stack.

Fifty component tests and 16 API/TCP tests pass without leaks. They include closing
an inbound parent while its outbound descendant remains uncertain, fence refusal
until the descendant retires, epoch/destination isolation, failed transfer,
unpublished cleanup, and capacity retained through reentrant release. The TCP
allocation-failure sweep uses retained dispatch and verifies one release after
rollback or signed terminal reconciliation. The final binary passes unchanged
with localhost access after two sandbox TCP failures. Evidence is recorded in
`remote-parent-retention-main-2c8240-oct14-application.json`.

Production query fanout, snapshots and response buffers still need adapters to
use these retained dispatches and accounted physical owners. Cyclic descendant
recovery and distributed shutdown require their full protocol; these tests do not
prove them. Production owned reads remain disabled and the full design remains
unfinished. Full qualification remains waived.


### Shared physical ownership for internal group queries (2026-10-14)

With runnable scheduling enabled, the production internal group-query route now
runs planning, schema routing, storage and encoding on the bounded backend
executor. It joins that physical future before handing off the response. The
query receives one general runnable root and passes its team through planning
into storage/graph controls. The worker lends CPU through existing wait/child
capabilities, then parks for output before waking the network waiter. Explicitly
disabled scheduling preserves the legacy handler; unavailable configured workers
reject rather than silently execute unbounded work on the network handler.

A stable owner funds request work through the general read allocation group when
the configured read pool exists (otherwise the bounded server heap). The response
retains the same group after worker completion. HTTP response destruction frees
its body before releasing the owner, heap group, runnable metadata and node pin.
Output backpressure consumes finite operation/heap capacity without keeping CPU.
This does not assert bounds for every storage-private/operator allocation.

Body timeouts are anchored at handler receipt, including time already spent
waiting. After bounded decoding, the owned root can only tighten that deadline
before publishing children. Schema routing now accepts the request allocator and
execution context: selected index names must be freed by the same group, and
metadata routing retains original execution authority. Query response formatting,
identity-read-generation headers, catalog fences and read-index consistency are
preserved. Memory pressure maps to availability rejection.

Five owner/production-handler tests, 98 scheduler tests (71 local plus 27 API),
and 143 query-contract tests pass without leaks. Coverage includes schema-selected
index allocation, physical snapshot scratch, control progress during CPU waits,
response lifetime, cancellation/shutdown cleanup, expired deadlines, allocation
failure, and bounded outstanding slow responses. Source and binary evidence is
in `internal-query-physical-owner-main-2c8240-oct14-application.json`.

This production route still uses the existing distributed transport. It does not
yet adopt the owned remote attempt/retained-parent protocol across remote query,
snapshot and child RPCs; that protocol remains unactivated for production reads.
Prior-process/cyclic recovery, complete private operator bounds and the other
full-design gaps remain open. Full qualification remains waived.


### Remote lease adapter for physical query owners (2026-10-14)

The API now exposes receipt-time read authentication/membership resolution
separately from later worker admission, preserving the verified deadline while
waiting for CPU. The query-owner adapter can adopt that verified lease before
query allocations or snapshots exist. Admission persists publication history
through its existing CPU wait boundary. The signed byte allowance caps the
owner and its query-allocation budget, including the bounded fallback allocator
when the read pool is absent. Duplicate/terminal admission never creates another
physical lease. This adapter is not a newly activated production owned-read RPC.

A composite descendant hold now retains worker authority, the query heap group
and runnable metadata together. Response retirement frees output first, detaches
the borrowed HTTP cancellation callback under a lifetime mutex, and latches an
owned stop signal. Descendants may outlive that HTTP context without reading it.
The final worker lease closes only after buffers, runnable metadata, the owner
allocation and node pin have retired. Additional snapshot/cursor ownership still
requires its own physical adapter; retaining an allocator does not free resources
owned elsewhere.

Outbox retention carries owned atomic cancellation signals and a fixed native
monotonic deadline. Reconciliation reads those while the slot pins their owner;
no borrowed request callback runs under the ledger mutex. Parent closure,
remote-worker cancellation or parent expiry select exact child cancellation but
retain charges until trustworthy physical terminal/fence evidence. Publication
rechecks parent cancellation after durable preparation. A query cannot tighten
its deadline after publishing remote child authority; routing/snapshot deadlines
are tightened before query work starts.

Eight query-owner tests, 52 component tests and 16 API/TCP tests pass without
leaks. The owner tests simulate HTTP-context destruction while a descendant stays
uncertain, enforce heap allowances in pooled and fallback modes, and check
active/duplicate/terminal admission. Components cover owned cancellation, expiry,
and cancellation during durable preparation. The unchanged API binary passes
with localhost access after two sandbox TCP failures. Evidence is recorded in
`internal-query-remote-owner-main-2c8240-oct14-application.json`.

Production owned-read registration/activation, outbound distributed query

### Authoritative membership checks on physical CPU resume (2026-10-14)

Remote query owners now require fresh membership validation at admission and
whenever a root, child or grandchild receives CPU after a quantum or I/O wait.
Each worker keeps independent validation state. Metadata calls lend CPU through
the same execution; their synchronous metadata-only children do not recursively
acquire the same proof. Validation preserves the original receipt deadline and
rechecks caller CPU-return restrictions after metadata I/O.

The API reads membership and the pinned reply public key from one owned
linearizable snapshot, with no observational fallback. Rejection stops runnable
execution and latches lease cancellation while retaining heap, worker and child
charges until physical cleanup. Seven append-only ABI details preserve membership
failure identities. Standalone borrowing test modules now import the platform
capacity dependency explicitly.

Scoped checks pass: 13 owner tests, 98 scheduler tests, 15 standalone borrowing,

binary required localhost access after two sandbox TCP failures; the unchanged

### Signed attempts enter the buffered group-query worker (2026-10-14)

The existing group-local buffered query route now accepts AFAT read credentials
through the shared service-auth ingress boundary. It captures the receipt clock
before authentication/body reads, verifies the exact method/path/body, and passes
the same deadline into CPU admission. Unsupported read routes remain closed to
attempt credentials. AFAT v1 does not bind routing headers or query parameters,
so these overrides and non-identity content encodings are rejected for signed
reads. Legacy service-authenticated queries preserve their existing behavior.

The worker bounds authoritative membership scratch before acquiring its lease.
The signed allowance covers the owner and retained input before the remaining
query heap budget; metadata scratch must be freed before physical admission.
Preparing a different receipt cannot refresh that deadline or budget. Worker
admission precedes semantic planning, backend snapshot work and query execution.
Active duplicates and terminal replays return 409 without another backend query.
The admitted lease and query heap remain charged through buffered output
retirement. Encoding checkpoints now use the same membership-aware borrowed
execution as backend work.

Fifteen owner/handler tests and 16 signed-RPC tests pass without leaks. Handler
coverage includes membership I/O and control progress, snapshot scratch, retained
output, duplicate/terminal replay, altered input, unbound routing overrides,
unsupported routes, wrong credential kind, expired ingress/admission, unavailable

### Owned group-query client and signed routing envelope (2026-10-14)

An API client adapter now sends buffered group queries through retained remote
attempt dispatch. The signed body contains an explicit version-1 envelope with
the query JSON, prepared-routing metadata and catalog route fence. Ingress decodes
this envelope with the admitted query allocator; unsigned routing headers remain
rejected. Prepared routing requires a fence and preserves the coordinator's
selected index through the routed table callback. Unknown/missing versions,
duplicate/unknown fields and empty queries fail closed. Legacy query bodies keep
their existing shape on the legacy path.

The adapter requires a trusted retained parent and an explicitly activated target.
Publication transfers that parent into the bounded outbox. Lost replies, non-200
responses and missing/invalid read-generation headers return uncertainty with the
original attempt identity. Even successful delivery does not release remote
credits: retirement still requires independently verified terminal/fence evidence.
Dispatch takes the earliest deadline from the retained parent, HTTP cancellation
and caller; an expired parent cannot publish and a later HTTP deadline cannot
extend it. Read buffers use the caller's allocator; control remains independently
accounted by the supplied protocol client. No legacy retry/fallback is introduced.

Response retirement now travels with moved query buffers from HTTP through the
client and native table QueryResponse. Buffers are freed before releasing their
physical owner. This also fixes existing public/group/graph client buffer moves
which previously could release that owner too early. Responses copied into a
different caller allocator can retire their original owner after the copy.

Nineteen owner/client/handler tests, 143 query-contract tests and 16 signed-RPC
tests pass without leaks. Coverage includes body-bound prepared index/fence
propagation, uncertainty across success/loss/HTTP or decode errors, parent deadline
composition, rejection before publication, and exact response-owner retirement.
The unchanged RPC binary passes with localhost access after two sandbox TCP
failures. Final-source hashes and logs are recorded in
`internal-query-owned-client-main-2c8240-oct14-application.json`.

### Retained authority through native buffered query routing (2026-10-14)

RequestContext and SearchRequest now carry a trusted native dispatch capability
for buffered group queries. Planning preserves it; query serialization excludes
it. The HTTP routing wrapper resolves the destination's catalog fence before
invoking the capability and clearing it from the transport request. Plain buffered
and streaming transports reject unconsumed capabilities before sending or changing
not-sent evidence. Vector-worker dispatch through this capability stays closed.

A query owner can bind a trusted protocol client. The buffered group-query handler
installs it only when owned state is recovered and at least one target has been
explicitly activated. Production targets remain unactivated. The callback matches
an unambiguous enrolled endpoint, signs the body-bound query/routing envelope,
and moves a parent hold into the outbox. Local holds retain the heap, scheduler
entry and node pin; inbound holds additionally retain the worker lease. Parent
cancellation and the fixed deadline propagate to reconciliation without releasing
uncertain credits. The child-publication marker is atomic for independent workers.

The byte charge is a fixed peer share (configured peer bytes divided by peer
attempt capacity). Idle-credit borrowing is not implemented here. A finite original
parent deadline is required. Oversized envelopes fail before publication. A lost,
non-200 or malformed reply remains uncertain; successful HTTP delivery also keeps
the outbox charge until independently verified retirement. Validated signed route
fences receive the normal acknowledgement. Absolute query deadlines now reach
transport cancellation metadata even when no cancellation token is present.
RemoteOutcomeUncertain has an append-only unavailable ABI detail.

Twenty-two owner/routing/handler tests, 143 query-contract tests, 32 error-ABI tests
and 16 signed-RPC tests pass without leaks. The owner tests cover successful, lost
and malformed replies for local and inbound parents, retain charges/heap after
root retirement, and release them only after modeled verified terminal evidence.
Routing checks prove prepared fence propagation, serialization exclusion, shorter
deadline preservation and rejection before unowned buffered/streaming sends.
The unchanged RPC binary passes with localhost access after two sandbox TCP
failures. Final-source evidence is recorded in
`internal-query-retained-routing-main-2c8240-oct14-application.json`.

### Retained public HTTP query owners (2026-10-14)

Internal and public owners share one retained dispatch adapter for routing,

Ordinary public single-query and NDJSON planning preserve the trusted capability.

### Physical retained-read admission lifetime (2026-10-14)

Retained read registry slots and per-principal counts now stay occupied until
snapshot/cursor/fence destruction returns. Revocation marks a single retiring
owner under the lock, invokes mandatory cleanup outside it, and frees the slot
only afterward. Concurrent/reentrant expiry, close and disconnect skip resources
already retiring, including cancellation pointers the destructor may have freed.
Shutdown closes admission before cancellation and cleanup; its existing
stop-ingress/join-request precondition remains required.

Capture, immutable snapshot and cursor factories now register an uninitialized
cancellation capsule and take an exclusive registry borrow before native backend
creation. Initialization fills optional physical handles while that borrow pins
the capsule. Publication validates lifetime, and failure/null/revocation closes
the reservation and initialized handles before capacity becomes reusable. The
small capsule allocation precedes insertion; native backend work never does.

### Retained-read RPC execution admission (2026-10-14)

Retained-read HTTP work now runs on admitted SQL workers with an execution
deadline anchored before handler authentication/parsing and worker queuing.

### Retained relational page admission (2026-10-14)

Retained-read page RPCs now lend their original execution context to the native
relational reader through a checked optional view callback. The reader scopes
that borrow to the synchronous page call, checks row/condition progress and
passes it to physical cursor and point reads. Storage I/O releases CPU through
the existing execution-wait boundary; CPU must be reacquired before rows return.
Failed or canceled page calls discard output and poison the retained cursor.
The borrow clears on every exit; the next call uses its own execution context.
The private API kernel ABI is version 33 for the appended view callback.

### Portable import publisher wait admission (2026-10-14)

### October 14: bounded node-owned retained-read retirement

`retained_read_retirement.zig` provides a bounded node ledger and one protected
consumer, with no per-capability worker. Reservations bound item/count/total
metadata bytes and retain the complete original execution/allocator/transport
parent chain before publication. Parent callbacks must charge the actual
execution and own stable references; they are not request-stack admission ports.

new allocation or worker. A fair cursor attempts at most one queued close and
one recovery observation per finite control pass, lending CPU through actual
transport I/O. Slot quota and parent charges survive physical resource free and
parent-pin release. Shutdown cannot destroy an undrained owner.

`Client.captureOwned` integrates this ledger with capture, snapshot and cursor
creation. Each child reserves its own obligation before invoking the executor;
returned handles store stable metadata on the node allocator. Close transfers
ownership instead of synchronously waiting or freeing an unresolved client.
Cleanup uses its own bounded scratch allocator and finite control authority,
not the foreground allocator, cancellation or expired deadline. Exact-token
pending/error results keep charges. A changed process enters needs_fence; only
re-observing authoritative retirement can clear it. Genuine unknown creations
remain charged and require signed recovery integration, not connection cancel
or timeout. A valid creation ACK's fixed token metadata is recorded before a
late original scope error, so that case can close its known capability without
exposing query output or replaying the creation.

### SQL setup ownership and cumulative read retirement charges (main fc4f2402)

request deadline before handing off to materialized fallback. If ownership is
still pending, it returns capacity pressure and retains the supervisor/pins.
Cancellation/timeout never authorize physical release. The observer has its own
capsule reference, and consumes setup rollback exactly once on either exit.

### Root-signed read capability discovery without activation or retirement

A separate capability probe now has its own AFAT request kind and protected

policy or a healthy response supplies no activation. The probe response itself
is an observation, not an admission grant or permanent protocol lease.

transport and optional wait boundary. Secure nonce generation can lend the

forAuthority rejects reuse for a changed key/root/reporter or expired scope.

node consumer must validate current authority/scope again before publishing one.

and capability signing clamps the normalized deadline rather than comparing

### Automatic bounded discovery on the node control consumer

The existing reconciliation consumer now alternates reconciliation and discovery
turns whenever its node client has a publication table. Each discovery turn
advances a destination cursor before I/O and performs at most one probe under
the lesser of the original pass deadline and configured RPC timeout. A failed
peer therefore cannot monopolize later probes or consume the next reconciliation
turn, including when max_rpc_calls is one. Clients without a publication table
continue using reconciliation turns only.

Discovery shares the consumer's independently reserved physical worker, cleanup
root and fixed 64 KiB per-pass scratch. It creates no request queue, connection
worker or additional idle operation. Runtime metadata growth is included in its
existing fixed baseline calculation. Probe cancellation uses the consumer's
original cancellation source; the publication ticket remains pending until the
synchronous transport has physically returned. Joining the consumer precedes
freeing the table or its node parents.

Only nonce-bound, authority-matched signed observations publish families. Any
probe failure clears that destination's permission for new captures while the
sticky owned-family requirement survives; already admitted resources retain
their copied descriptor and original retirement obligations. Discovery never
advances a generation or retires a data charge. Snapshot counters distinguish
discovery turns/failures and last selected destination from reconciliation
passes and generation advances.

The periodic native/imported-worker fixture supplies explicit trusted signed
support to exercise publication and invalidation. This is not yet evidence of
positive production readiness advertisement, live distributed SQL/storage
integration, process replacement or permanent-loss retirement. The native family
advertisement policy and owned protocol flags remain disabled by default.

### Receiver discovery admission and fixed control bodies

A node-wide, fail-fast discovery admission has capacity one, separate from the
shared protected control admission. Capability ingress acquires it before body
receipt, context allocation or protected CPU admission. Successful authentication
moves the lease into the physical control context. It survives output parking
and is released only after that context is destroyed. Early failure releases all
provisional ownership. This bounds overlapping observers from all coordinators
at this receiver; status, cancel and fence do not consume the discovery lease.

Protected routes also set transport-level body limits: 32 bytes for a capability
nonce and two bytes for the exact control body. Oversized bodies are rejected
with HTTP 413 before protocol parsing. These limits do not change valid wire
requests. They bound this admission path; complete transport/metadata dependency
isolation and multi-node burst qualification remain broader design work.

Direct and opaque registrars share the canonical postBodyLimit policy. The
opaque manifest validates each requested fixed limit against that policy, and
the host installs it on its real router. The startup fixture now inspects the
opaque host's registered limits; its final verification remains in flight.

### Bind owned reads to the enrolled process

Owned data dispatch now uses distinct group query and retained-read routes whose
URI includes the enrolled durable root and reporter incarnation. AFAT authenticates
the entire scoped URI. The receiver checks both identities before membership
lookup or data execution. Legacy-only routers cannot match the new paths, and
the new handlers require authenticated owned ingress plus runnable admission.
A restarted process sharing the durable root cannot execute a request addressed
to the previous reporter. Existing status, cancel and fence protocols retain
their independent retirement rules.

Capability advertisements now use AFAC version 2 to promise these scoped routes;
version 1 advertisements are rejected. This leaves AFAT and retirement evidence
versions unchanged. Sender path allocation occurs after ledger reservation and
parent attachment, preserving allocation-failure ownership and bounding the
metadata lifetime. Cleanup uses protected control allocation and the same
process-scoped retained-read route.

### Publish peer views without rebinding outstanding work

The node now owns a bounded publication source. A query dispatcher registers its
unique operation before planning and retains that operation's endpoint view
through physical root retirement. The reconciler resolves nonzero operations

evidence verification and buffer destruction. Generation/startup fencing keeps
its existing protocol. Publishing a different reporter or URI never certifies
physical retirement of old work.

positive publication records shared, sticky activation before exposing family
bits, so refresh cannot restore unowned legacy dispatch. The periodic consumer
holds the current view through discovery and publication. New bindings,
publication and control leases keep their metadata owner alive through physical
return. All source/binding allocations reserve node control baseline bytes first;
capacity failure publishes nothing, and close/deinit retain pending ownership.

to new reads without removing durable indices or retiring obligations. A changed
root/key/index requires separate durable topology evolution; this component only
refreshes the already enrolled root set. Failed refresh invalidates stale

publication is rejected for metadata capacity, old roots can still clean up at
a same-process address. New data eligibility remains closed until ordinary
publication and capability discovery succeed.

still update an authenticated address. Reporter/key/root changes never redirect
old-process cleanup or imply physical retirement.

that leave the data view unchanged. This fences slower publishers and handles
URI reversion after a previous allocation failure. A rejected stale cut changes
nothing. Existing native and opaque refresh share these rules; bootstrap
preflight includes route table storage and the corrected consumer scratch.

### Prepared independent remote-cleanup ownership migration (not applied)

The current pgwire owner still retains ordinary query admission and foreground connection memory until its remote retirement pins finish. This contradicts the original requirement that uncertain remote attempts must not pin ordinary local request slots. The proposed migration moves registry/outbox references, node pins and the original endpoint binding into a bounded node-owned owner, independent of the SQL session, input arena and admission lease. Direct dispatch must move its release context and cancellation atomic as well; transferring only the registry parent would leave outbox pointers into the destroyed foreground owner. Nested fallible pin, parent-retain and resource-poll callbacks also require checked error translation across separately compiled images.

Prepared artifacts under the cumulative-integration receipt directory, all syntax-checked only and **not applied, compiled or runtime verified**:

- `remote-read-independent-owner-complete-migration-main-d0614ed7e5-draft.patch`: six-file core/owner/dispatcher/pgwire/test-consumer migration, including early/late ACK setup regressions and registry/outbox release ordering. The focused pgwire filter explicitly selects the new owner cases.
- `sql-tcp-post-handler-response-loss-main-d0614ed7e5-support-draft.patch`: installs fixture middleware before listener startup; shuts down the real HTTP/1 socket only after the production handler returns.
- `sql-tcp-post-handler-response-loss-main-d0614ed7e5-integration-draft.patch`: single-admission SQL test requiring foreground release, an actual materialized `SELECT 1` with a fresh deadline while original remote charges remain, and bounded physical retirement after replies resume. Normal remote fixture cleanup also separates foreground retirement from physical remote retirement.

Application must wait for the current baseline native runner to terminate. Then validate component base hashes, compile and run the focused pgwire/owner cases, and run the actual provisioned TCP fixture. A healthy third remote destination, refusal before publication when the failed destination is exhausted, and actual separately compiled API/host boundary tests remain necessary. ### Bounded FIFO remote credits before publication

Applied bounded intrusive destination FIFO waits to the coordinator and client. Queue length is at most min(ledger slots, 64), with a separate per-destination bound; queued allowance is overflow-checked and reported separately from charged attempt bytes. New callers cannot steal a destination credit ahead of its waiters. Queueing creates no attempt ID, journal entry, transport publication, or task. The client uses only the original request execution-wait boundary and deadline, checking parent cancellation on each probe. A generation change rejects the old waiter. Fence-capture ports prohibit waiting; only a signed creation proved absent may return backpressure so the statement owner can release all partial fences before retrying.

Added an isolated control admission foundation, not yet connected to node RPCs.
It preallocates all FIFO entries under a control baseline before publishing the
owner, reuses the common admission controller, keeps uncontrolled calls
fail-fast, preserves the original deadline/cancellation and balances CPU parking
and reentry. Allocation failure returns the entire reservation; refused live
destruction preserves it. Native tests pass for allocation rollback and live

`remote-control-admission-foundation-native-v1` (2/2, no skips/failures/leaks).

Control admission must precede credential construction so signed remaining

Starting a 250ms cleanup root before a longer queue wait is not a progress proof.
No node control policy or RPC call site has changed yet; actual C1 liveness and
all broader outstanding requirements remain unverified.


### Worker progress telemetry envelope (2026-10-16)

Worker progress is advisory and can run while the native team is still
computing. It must not use an acknowledged output event or release that team's
CPU grant as though the whole team had stopped. The child now uses a per-request
atomic gate: one reporting callback may enter the transport, with successful
entries separated by at least 100 ms of native monotonic time. Overlapping and
rate-limited reports are dropped without waiting, allocating, spawning tasks or
retrying; these reports are not a lossless stream or a latest-value mailbox.
Terminal results still use the existing independent response path.

Progress JSON encoding now uses fixed 2 KiB stack storage instead of a
caller-sized allocation. Model/backend labels are capped at 256/32 bytes,
matching the enrichment status fields. Truncation preserves UTF-8 boundaries;
invalid diagnostic prefixes are omitted. Maximum JSON escaping and integer
widths fit that buffer. The wire event schema and public ABI are unchanged.
One gate belongs to each live RPC Request and remains owned through its join.

`worker-progress-native-v4` passes all 27 focused build steps on macOS:
three direct helper cases, thirty RPC cases (including those same three helper
cases), six production parent-phase cases, six wire cases, two physical owner
handoff cases and two HTTP-control cases. The new real-pipe production callback
case delivers capped labels, suppresses 1,000 overlapping reports, preserves the
terminal response and rejects any attempted phase handoff. These are overlapping
selections, not independent contract counts. `worker-progress-verified.json`
rehashes the current native/schema inputs and receipt/log and checks the actual
named-case inventories. Early runs are excluded: v1 named a nonexistent build
step; v2 exposed duplicate module ownership; v3 exposed a test parameter shadow.
The restricted runs also failed loopback setup: a direct bind returned EPERM.
The final run enabled local networking and passed the real TCP cases.

This change does not prove complete progress-stage admission. The first reporter
still uses the ordinary RPC offer/pipe path; its wait is not bounded by the
100 ms rate gate. Parent progress still calls enrichment's
`noteInferenceProgress`, which takes the coordinator mutex with an uncancelable
wait and then invokes the activity hook. That path needs independently charged
control execution and bounded synchronization, without parking the live native
team's CPU. The encoding ceiling does not qualify arbitrary callback CPU, all
native stack/private-heap costs, Linux behavior, or production scheduling
defaults. The earlier separately compiled API integration predates this batch.
The full design remains active and incomplete.


### Enrichment progress mailbox and lifecycle retirement (2026-10-16)

The production enrichment progress callback no longer enters the coordinator
mutex or invokes its activity hook. It copies one advisory sample into a fixed
mailbox using one atomic try-lock attempt. A contended publisher drops its
report; accepted reports replace the pending sample. Model/backend labels are
copied into 256/32-byte UTF-8 prefixes, without retaining caller slices or
allocating. Empty detail reports preserve pending labels and deadline metadata.
The direct helper test asserts the mailbox's native size is at most 512 bytes.
This is a per-runtime telemetry slot, not another worker, parked task or queue.

Live `stats` readers and ordinary activity boundaries consume the sample while
owning the coordinator mutex. Consumption itself never waits for a publisher.
The reporting callback performs no scheduler checkpoint and cannot release a
still-computing native team's CPU loan. Deadline projection is captured at report
time, rather than renewed when the sample is consumed. Phase completion,
publication, clear, joined stop, restart preparation and detached reload
invalidate queued samples. A generation captured before the callback's clock
reads rejects an obsolete report even if its publication races a transition.
Callbacks still borrow the runtime through the existing physical provider join;
the mailbox retains no observer callback or borrowed model strings.

The joined-stop test first failed on the actual implementation: a queued sample
restored `.executing` after the real `stop` boundary. That failure is preserved
in `enrichment-progress-stop-before-v1`. Invalidation after provider/replay join
now makes the same test pass. The held-mutex production test calls the actual
reporter on a separate thread while the coordinator mutex is held, observes its
completion before releasing that mutex, and verifies no activity hook ran.
The ordinary owning activity boundary then consumes the sample and invokes the
hook after unlocking. Other cases cover 1,000 coalesced updates, copied label
ownership, generation rejection, contention, UTF-8 and clock-domain projection.

`enrichment-progress-native-v2` passes all 70 focused build steps on current
native/schema inputs. Its mailbox selection has seven bodies: two production
runtime cases, three helper cases, one existing clock case and the root's
anonymous discovery body. The same run passes 21 existing derived visibility
wait cases, thirty worker RPC cases (including three gate-helper cases), six
production parent-phase cases, six wire cases, three direct gate-helper cases,
two physical H1/H2 owner cases and two HTTP-control cases. These overlapping
selections are not independent requirement counts. The verifier
`enrichment-progress-verified.json` checks current source/schema/receipt/log
hashes, actual named contracts, aggregate counts and the preserved stop failure.
Formatting and whitespace checks pass. No C ABI or worker wire version changed.

Progress delivery remains incomplete at the full-design scope. Live status
reads consume the mailbox during inference. Subsequent source audit confirmed
an existing one-second runtime-status owner also polls snapshots marked as
pending. The earlier statement that cached updates happen only at ordinary
lifecycle boundaries was too strong. The refresh-admission follow-up below
addresses missing active-phase polling and shared CPU admission; downstream
snapshot/publication waits still need bounded ownership.
The mailbox does not qualify independent control CPU admission, arbitrary
external progress targets, elapsed/native stack/private-heap profiles, or the
first reporter's ordinary RPC offer/pipe wait. It deliberately does not invoke
those unbounded hooks from a live native team's report callback. Existing
publication/repair notifications retain their ordinary paths and semantics.
Linux, current separately compiled API integration and production defaults are
not qualified by this macOS focused run. The full original goal remains active.


### Shared admission for the existing runtime-status owner (2026-10-16)

The existing data runtime already coalesces refreshes into one joined durable
job and re-arms its dirty latch while observed work remains pending. It polls
at one-second cadence. That owner is now the independent consumer of enrichment
progress; no new registry, reporting thread or borrowed subscriber callback was
added. Active enrichment phases and active batch items keep refresh debt live
even when the replay target has caught up. Live stats consumption therefore
continues through executing, serializing and publishing phases without invoking
observers from a still-computing native team's report callback.

Each queued refresh records one native two-second cooperative deadline before
submission. Coalesced wakes cannot renew it. The queued job reads the already
published backend runtime rather than entering backend registration/cache locks
before admission. Where shared scheduling is enabled, it acquires one background
CPU slot and charges pass metadata plus the execution capsule. Scheduler waiting
uses the original deadline and existing bounded admission wait. It leaves the
protected control lane available. Explicitly disabled scheduling retains legacy
execution while still observing the finite budget and shutdown signal. A
provided owner that rejects admission does not trigger an uncharged fallback.

The collector checks the same pass at observation boundaries, table/group
iterations and before cache publication. Expiry, cancellation, admission failure
or incomplete collection retains dirty debt. Failure defers a new attempt for
one second, including rejection by the durable-job queue itself. Retry deferral
is published before releasing the singleflight latch. Retry/shutdown checks are
repeated under the refresh publication mutex: a wake that passed optimistic
checks cannot replace a newer retry fence or publish work during shutdown.
A deterministic thread test first reproduced that race: a wake paused at the
mutex attempted submission into a paused durable owner instead of deferring.
The preserved before-run reports expected null versus BackgroundOwnerPaused;
the fixed contract passes for both retry and shutdown modes.

The original job owner retains the DataServer/backend through physical return.
The execution capsule finishes only after synchronous observations and their
cleanup return. Cancellation/deadline signals do not release capacity while an
observation is still running. The helper tests use actual scheduler capsules:
a refresh queues behind a held foreground reservation, health admission still
succeeds, and refresh admission succeeds after release. A cancellation case
observes its operation/CPU still charged until physical return/finish. Five real
DataServer contract cases exercise expiry, missing-runtime refusal without lazy
initialization, coalesced deadlines, budget rejection before metadata, active
phase polling, durable queue rejection and the concurrent wake race with
controlled fixtures. They do not start a live Raft host, model, or API image.

`status-refresh-admission-native-v7` passes all 68 focused build steps on current
native/schema inputs. Actual logged bodies are three scheduler-pass contracts,
twelve data-suite bodies (five named contracts and seven anonymous discovery
bodies), one supplemental common-owner discovery body, and seven mailbox-suite
bodies (six existing named cases and one root discovery body). The derived
visibility target is cached success; this run is not a fresh 21-case visibility
proof. The two new targeted suites force execution, and the data cases are also

`status-refresh-admission-verified.json` rehashes current native/schema inputs,
receipt/logs and all eight new contract names, and binds the actual failing
concurrent-wake receipt. Source formatting and whitespace checks pass.

Earlier v1/v2 excluded runs compiled the data tests but failed their direct
Mach-O object link (compiler runtime and unrelated Raft teardown symbols).
The attempted object compiler-runtime switch did not resolve that closure and
was removed. The final focused suite uses a normal Zig test executable and
explicitly retires the storage fixtures it initializes; no Raft/listener owner is
created. v3 established the first passing data cases; v4 added bounded retry,
v5 fixed the reproduced wake race, v6 removed worker-side backend registration,
and v7 covers durable-queue rejection as well. No C ABI or worker wire layout
changed. No current separately compiled API-image or Linux claim follows.

This does not qualify fully bounded notification delivery. Deep metadata/DB
calls and lock waits can overrun the cooperative deadline; their physical
ownership remains charged until they return. Catalog cloning, status snapshots
and private heaps are not covered by the pass-metadata charge. The subsequent table-paging work below addresses resumption between
tables; whole-catalog preparation and collection within one table remain
unbounded. Actual end-to-end model progress,
opaque archive/transport lifetime propagation, supported-envelope elapsed and
memory profiles, SDK/operator families, fair default qualification and the
original adaptive/durable/recovery requirements remain outstanding. The full
original goal stays active; full resource qualification remains waived rather
than inferred from these scoped checks.

### Resumable status-refresh table pages

The refresh owner now attempts at most eight tables per admitted pass. A numeric
cursor records each attempt before fallible collection and retains a fixed upper
table-ID fence for the sweep. Expiry or a bad observation therefore cannot force
every later pass to restart at the first table. New high IDs join the next sweep;
metadata changes and unfinished work retain refresh debt. Completed tables publish
immediately, while every unpublished owned status is retired on error.

Absence pruning uses the full authoritative presence set separately from sampled
payload replacement. Unsampled present tables keep their cached facts. Both table
publication and absence removal inherit epochs captured before the catalog read;
per-table paging cannot acquire fresh lifecycle authority after intervening DDL.
Cold cache entries can be initialized only without a competing lifecycle or cache
invalidation. Per-entry append and table-name allocation failures retire their
payloads, and returned counters are finalized before the return value is copied.

Focused tests cover growing catalogs, failed/deleted attempts, retained unsampled
facts, independent absence pruning, partial progress before expiry, cold/cache-only
refresh without DB opens, lifecycle races, and collection allocation failures.
`status-refresh-paging-native-v5` passes all 87 focused build steps on unchanged
native/schema inputs. The verifier checks all twelve new named contracts: four
DataServer paging cases, three cursor cases, and five cache lifecycle/pruning
cases. Actual inventories include fourteen data-paging bodies, eight cache bodies
(the five new cases plus three existing structural-publication regressions),
twelve admission bodies, three scheduler-pass contracts and seven mailbox bodies,
with no failures or leaks. The visibility target is cached success, not a new
21-case run. `status-refresh-paging-verified.json` binds current input hashes and
the receipt/log. Earlier admission receipts describe their recorded revision.

The first paging runs exposed fixture backend ownership and returned-counter
issues; both are fixed. The first API cache run exposed a test that incorrectly
assumed ordinary publication advances topology; the corrected test separately
checks uncaptured table retention and real lifecycle invalidation. Cache contracts
are selected through their API owner, since data-module selectors did not discover
them. The default API-derived coverage suite already owns the whole cache suite;
default data selection includes the new paging and cursor cases.

This bounds attempted tables, not table size or total refresh memory/time. The
metadata snapshot, ownership/presence preparation, cache-token capture and absence
pruning still scale with catalog size. Collection of groups within one table and
deep synchronous observations still need resumable bounded stages and memory
accounting. No Linux, compiled-image, production-envelope or full-design completion
claim follows from this step.

### Resumable group observations

The status owner now attempts at most eight groups in total per admitted pass,
within the existing eight-table ceiling. It retains a numeric cursor within the
current table, fixes the group's upper-ID fence for that visit, and records each
attempt before fallible collection. A failed group does not restart the next
pass at earlier groups. Each completed group publishes immediately using the
premetadata table/target/observation fences. Its owned payload is released after
the cache publication boundary. Partial publication preserves unsampled sibling
facts rather than treating an observation fragment as a complete table.

Authoritative group presence is pruned separately, at most eight retired payloads
per call. A newer publication or changed lifecycle retains retry debt. A table
observation-generation floor rejects older single/batch/refresh callbacks after
retirement, preventing an old callback from restoring a deleted group. Retired
payloads are destroyed outside the cache mutex. The read mirror is withdrawn
before reconstruction so empty tables or allocation failure cannot expose deleted
groups to new readers. Existing readers retain their already-owned snapshots.

Tests exercise within-table resumption, preservation of unsampled sibling facts,
resumption after expiry, bounded absence retirement, stale callback rejection,
newer publication retention, lifecycle changes and empty read-view retirement.
`status-refresh-groups-native-v2` passes all 87 focused build steps on unchanged
native/schema inputs, with sixteen data-paging bodies, ten cache bodies, twelve
admission bodies, three scheduler-pass contracts and seven mailbox bodies. No
failures or leaks are reported. `status-refresh-groups-verified.json` checks all
sixteen named paging contracts against source, rehashes current native/schema
inputs and binds the receipt/log. The visibility target remains cached success;
this is not a fresh 21-case visibility run. Formatting and whitespace checks pass.
Earlier table-paging receipts retain their recorded revision's scope. No ABI or
worker-wire layout changed. Separately compiled images, Linux, default envelopes
and the original full design are not qualified by these focused checks.

This is a bound on observation attempts and retired payload count. Metadata and
presence sets still allocate in proportion to catalog/table size. Candidate scans,
read-view reconstruction, targeted-index handoff reductions and destruction of a
single status may still scale with group/index count. These stages need cursors,
explicit accounting and elapsed/memory profiles before claiming bounded control
notification delivery or qualified defaults. A single synchronous observation
still has a cooperative deadline, not a proven hard return bound. All remaining
original design requirements stay active; full heavyweight qualification remains
waived.

### Incremental read-view retirement

Group absence cleanup no longer withdraws and reconstructs the entire read view.
Its fixed eight-entry scratch now also owns detached read-group references.
Immutable slot positions and allocation size remain valid for retained view
readers; retirement clears individual payload slots under the read mutex and
releases them after leaving cache locks. New snapshots compact only live slots,
and an all-empty view returns no status. Single and partial-group publication
can refill an existing slot without rebuilding siblings. Adding a new group ID
or a genuine lifecycle replacement still rebuilds topology.

The focused allocation regression arms the cache allocator to fail at its next
allocation, retires a group, and verifies no allocation was attempted and no
sibling read payload was cloned or replaced. A previously pinned payload survives
retirement and is released outside both cache mutexes. A concurrent production
snapshot regression pauses before and after payload pinning: a reader that has
not pinned the retired payload omits it; a reader that already pinned it finishes
with its owned historical snapshot. Partial publication then refills the empty
slot. `status-refresh-read-retirement-native-v2` passes all 87 focused build
steps on unchanged native/schema inputs. Actual inventories are thirteen cache
cases (nine new paging contracts plus four existing structural/read-payload
regressions), sixteen data-paging bodies, twelve admission bodies, three scheduler
contracts and seven mailbox bodies, with no failures or leaks. The independent
`status-refresh-read-retirement-verified.json` checks all eighteen named paging
contracts, the existing read-payload ownership regression and current input/log
hashes. Visibility-target success remains cached, not a fresh 21-case execution.
Formatting and whitespace checks pass. The preceding v1 verifies allocation and
sibling preservation; v2 adds the actual concurrent reader and partial-slot refill
cases. No ABI or worker-wire layout changed.

Slot/index storage remains at the current topology's allocated capacity until a
later topology replacement; retirement releases the deep group payloads. This
removes a full-table clone/rebuild from group pruning, but does not bound reader
snapshot work, candidate scans, metadata/presence allocation, targeted authority
reductions or a single payload's index bytes/destruction. New-ID topology growth
still needs staged construction and explicit accounting. Current compiled images,
Linux/default envelopes and all remaining original design requirements remain
unqualified; the full goal stays active.

### Child RPC slabs and request heaps join the node owner (October 16)

The parent now reserves node memory for each incoming child payload before
publishing its offer. A fixed 256-entry table retains that grant through response
delivery, cancellation and uncertain transport failure. The child reports
retirement only after physically freeing the receive slab. Unknown retirement
IDs close the transport without refunding unrelated credit. Confirmed rejection before allocation
can refund its receive grant; EOF alone cannot. The parent's physical
kill-and-reap fence releases any remaining grants.

Child request/create arenas, serialization and generated output slabs now use a
retained allocator backed by dedicated resource RPC. Its growth is admitted by
the actual node ledger before backing allocation, using one stable identity per
worker generation. Free releases node credit after physical allocator free.
Accepted credit survives a lost reply until reap. Invalid replies, uncertain
transport outcomes and refused retirement exit immediately, bypassing libc
teardown; the surviving parent retains responsibility for physical quiescence.
The same parent apply/retire functions serve production and the real-ledger test.

Growth parks an existing borrowed execution scope and rejoins it before backing
allocation. Mandatory free does not depend on reacquiring ordinary execution
capacity. Resource replies and payload-retirement notifications use the existing
dedicated control path. Allocation/free that can perform resource RPC runs
outside the endpoint reader mutex, so the reader can route its replies.

Private worker framing advances to AFW5 and worker wire version 12. C ABI versions
remain API 48, inference-host 38 and local-inference 4. Old worker processes fail
the framing/version gate rather than silently omitting retirement accounting.

`worker-child-memory-native-v5` passes all 82 focused build steps. The verifier
matches seventy-eight named cases: thirty-nine RPC/progress, twenty
worker/provider/ABI/control, eight actual node-ledger, ten subprocess lifecycle
and one production standalone callback/owner-lifetime case. It binds 4,614 native
and Python inputs, 32 schema inputs, the runner and log hashes. The new actual
node-ledger test exercises the same parent helper as production, dedicated child
heap RPC, query/storage pressure, capacity refusal/retry and retained response
retirement. Existing rejection and mid-transfer cancellation fixtures now enable
peer grants and assert refund while preserving nested-call progress. Additional
cases gate physical receive free, reject unknown receipts, bound zero-byte grant
metadata and inject a malformed heap reply into a real subprocess with wedged
libc teardown. The production child entry point is semantically compiled; full
model execution and a current linked production image remain unqualified.

V3's first shared-helper extraction caught two value-versus-pointer compilation
errors. V4 corrected them; V5 extends rejection/cancellation coverage. Earlier
receipts remain historical. No failure, skip or leak remains in the final cases.
These changes cover child receive slabs and the selected handler-owned heaps.
Reader/control bookkeeping, remaining RPC/header/container and fixed owner
metadata, backend/process reservations outside existing contracts and complete
frontend/operator/query accounting still need work. Whole-node crash and
external-operation quiescence, durable completion, adaptive policy and the
original default fairness/overload profiles remain outstanding. Full heavyweight
qualification remains waived; current Linux/production images and full-design
completion are not claimed.

### Worker fixed control state and startup admission (October 16)

Resource-frame dispatch now reuses 128 inline task slots per endpoint instead of
allocating a task for each callback. A slot stays occupied through callback and
physical reply write, then becomes available under the endpoint mutex. Duplicate
IDs and slot exhaustion retain the existing fail-and-reap behavior. Ordinary
payload quotas and endpoint allocator exhaustion cannot consume these slots.
Runtime task/stack creation still has its independent failure contract.

The parent serializes resource parsing under its existing resource mutex using
8 KiB of fixed scratch stored in the Worker. Resource request and operation JSON
parsing no longer require the parent heap. The one-KiB resource-frame limit still
applies; parsing failure fences the worker before the resource operation runs.
Existing lease-map growth and new cache-observation metadata can still allocate
before their respective mutations and remain separate work.

Before allocating or spawning a generation, Client reserves the platform-specific
sum of `@sizeOf(Worker)`, `@sizeOf(Child)` and the child's PayloadBudget from the
same authoritative node transient-memory hook. This covers the newly fixed
resource task tables and parent parser scratch along with those objects' other
inline fields. The identity lives in the Client, outside the generation being
allocated. Refusal occurs before Worker allocation. Failed startup unwinds the

returning its baseline; a disconnected endpoint cannot make it reusable early.
This is accounted fixed-state memory, not a whole-process RSS bound.

### Worker lease and cache metadata ownership (October 16)

Each generation now owns a separate PayloadBudget with a 1 MiB derived-allocation
ceiling and no ordinary small-message allowance. It retains the node context and
uses the same authoritative transient-host adjustment hook before backing
allocation. Lease-map storage, observation-pointer arrays and stable observation
objects allocate and free through this budget. Ordinary payloads cannot consume
its private allowance; both allowances still enforce the same aggregate node
limit. Existing map/list capacity remains charged until physical container free,
including after its last entry is removed. Reallocation charges the simultaneous
old and new allocations. This is a separate ceiling, not an extra node envelope
or a promise of fresh allocations after aggregate node exhaustion.

Lease tracking capacity is acquired before reserving a model admission lease.
Metadata quota/backing refusal returns explicit temporary capacity failure
without calling reserve. New cache observation capacity and its object are owned
before the upstream callback. The object is published only after callback
success; denial frees the unpublished object, leaving only accounted reusable
container capacity. Retirement and reaped cleanup use the original allocator and
need no fresh metadata allocation. Startup baseline now includes two
PayloadBudget objects: the child request heap and parent resource metadata.
Metadata context release and physical object destruction precede baseline return.

Cache refusal semantics are distinct. Tokenizer growth has a refusal path before
publication. Prompt-cache updates report memory already retained through a void
observer; ignoring a refusal would let the child continue with unreported bytes.
The production child now takes its immediate fatal ownership boundary for any
refused prompt-cache observation, and for a refused shrink of either cache type.
The parent joins/reaps before returning its surviving recorded reservations.
This closes continued execution after an observation failure; it does not turn
observational backend caches into strict reserve-before-allocation accounting.

### Worker RPC transport metadata ownership (October 16)

RPC pending/active/offer/incoming maps, Request objects and queued Message
containers now use an explicit transport metadata allocator. This allocator is
separate from resource lease/cache tracking and from payload bytes. Allocation
provenance is preserved through removal, cancellation, reader shutdown and
endpoint destruction; reusable container capacity stays charged until physical
free. Empty events consume metadata credit even when their payload uses zero
bytes. The existing 1,024-message queue ceiling now has a checked finish guard
as well as offer admission, rather than relying solely on a debug assertion.

The parent's generation owns a separate 1 MiB transport PayloadBudget, using the
node transient-host hook before backing allocations. The child uses a local
2 MiB transport PayloadBudget without synchronous peer callbacks. Parent startup
precharges that entire child allowance to the same node ledger before spawning;
it remains held through child reap and endpoint/object destruction. The reader
therefore never needs to issue a resource RPC to allocate bookkeeping needed for
routing resource replies. Growth of incoming-map storage is admitted before the
receiver allocates or accepts a slab; refusal rejects the offer without creating
a retirement receipt. Caller-side map refusal returns temporary capacity before
publication. Dedicated resource tasks/replies still use their existing fixed
storage and remain independent of ordinary transport metadata exhaustion.

The baseline is now `@sizeOf(Worker) + @sizeOf(Child) +
4 * @sizeOf(PayloadBudget) + child_metadata_limit`: child request and transport
budgets plus parent resource and transport budgets, their inline owners and the
precharged child transport allowance. Parent dynamic allocations remain charged
by actual live bytes; the child allowance is conservatively reserved in full.
This is a logical owned-memory reservation, not a whole-process resident bound.

Private worker wire advances to 13 and framing to AFW6 so older child processes
cannot silently bypass the reader metadata ceiling. API 48, inference-host 38
and local-inference 4 remain unchanged.

### Parent worker HTTP marshaling and response descriptors (October 16)

Parent worker HTTP dispatch now requires a configured node budget before reading

parsing use the same allocator. Event decoding uses a freeing allocator rather
than accumulating every frame in a long-lived arena. Controlled child event JSON
now uses the endpoint compute allocator, matching uncontrolled event serialization
and entering the child heap's node admission path before backing allocation.

also allocate from that budget. The owner retains allocator lifetime even for a
static error body after all headers are removed. A received body keeps its
original slab; the owner holds that payload through response destruction. The
production HTTP ABI publisher now shares a testable consuming function: response
state and header-view descriptors use the selected allocator, and the public HTTP
response destructor frees them after response cleanup. No response handle is
published until all allocations succeed. Worker-path allocation refusal becomes
temporary capacity at the HTTP boundary; other causes retain their identity.
Provider marshaling now uses the same configured-budget preflight.

capacity alone does not establish a low-latency SQL benefit.

The concrete scheduler gap found during this audit was unbounded queue traversal
under the scheduler mutex. Both the initial eligibility probe and deficit-round
candidate selection could inspect the entire class queue. Each now examines the

from `max_backfills`, which still limits how many grants may bypass a blocked head.
An exhausted window preserves the existing paid-team drain barrier. A fitting
operation outside that window becomes visible as earlier entries retire; usable
capacity can intentionally idle until the bounded window admits a fitting entry.
There is no new configuration field or ABI layout.

### Prepared memory batch admission (October 16)

The full-design multi-resource bundle remains incomplete. Its memory component
now has `ResourceManager.prepareBatch` and
`PreparedBatchReservation.tryAcquire`. Preparation installs ownership metadata
outside executor locks and holds no working-set capacity. A try-acquire uses
only try-locks and preinstalled identity lookup: it validates every normalized
slice and the local aggregate, then attempts the full ancestor memory charge
through the existing nonblocking parent ABI. Ancestor admission is the last
fallible action. Busy, denied, unsupported, intrinsic-size, and stale-token
results leave working-set ownership unchanged. Success moves the same identity
into an ordinary `BatchReservation` without an insertion or allocation.

Prepared metadata cannot release or reduce an active reservation, and a stale
prepared copy cannot remove the identity after acquisition. Unused metadata
retirement happens outside executor locks because ledger removal can compact
the hash table. Queued metadata still requires operation-admission coverage;
this API does not itself bound the number of queued preparations. The existing
production reservation callers have not been switched to this API.

`antfly-prepared-memory-batch-test` passed 20/20 build steps and 10/10 tests in
ReleaseSafe on macOS. The exact compiled binary was also run directly to verify
all named cases: four new prepared-admission cases, five existing identity/batch
regressions, and one declaration-discovery anchor. Coverage includes held local
and ancestor accounting/notification locks across three managers, allocator
refusal after preparation, local and shared-parent denial, changed hard limits,
request-size classification, unsupported parents, stale/forged ownership,
metadata OOM, overflow, and exact release. Receipts, named-case output, and
source snapshots are in the cumulative integration receipt directory under
`prepared-memory-native-v3.*`, `prepared-memory-verified.json`, and
`prepared-memory-source-snapshots.json`. V1 records a test teardown compilation
error; V2 passed nine cases; V3 adds preparation OOM/overflow coverage.

Next, establish independently discoverable continuation/cleanup progress before
adding fresh-start resource probes to the bounded CPU candidate window. A
continuation retaining memory must not be hidden behind starts waiting for that
same memory. CPU, memory, and I/O must then commit as one bundle, with complete
rollback of any tentative I/O credit before waiting. CPU parking must retain
physical memory and live I/O charges until their owners retire. These changes,
the full-design age barrier, and measured class service remain open; these ten
local tests establish none of those broader guarantees. Full heavyweight
qualification remains waived, and the original 731-line design remains the
completion authority.


### Independent continuation discovery (October 16)

The production CPU selector now separates each class's fresh-start and
continuation lists. Both bounded selection passes merge their candidates by
existing enqueue sequence and charge the same deficit credit. Each population
has a head-plus-eight window; together a class inspects at most eighteen entries
per pass. No queue length can expand either window. The earliest merged head
continues to govern CPU backfill barriers and paid-team drain. Control/cleanup
selection, read-lane weight presence, CPU borrowing/return checks, queue removal,
and shutdown all see both populations. The lists remain caller-owned and
allocation-free. This adds internal queue heads and an entry flag; public runtime
ABI/configuration layouts are unchanged.

First grants mark subsequent reentry as continuation work. Reentry from a parked
state and physical cleanup transfer also select that population. In particular,
a reserved child can already hold external resources before receiving its first
CPU grant; its initial return must not be treated as a fresh start. The new test
covers that path through the real reserve-child API and verifies original parent
ownership and retained metadata survive it.

Four new scheduler contracts verify shared/isolated lanes and resource/output
parking with a full fresh-start window, preserve merged FIFO service and yielding
without unconditional continuation priority, close a queued continuation while
joining a live fresh start, bound continuation scanning independently of a
visible fresh candidate, and admit a reserved child's first return. Existing
weighted teams, loan conversion/return, read demotion, original authority,
cancellation, accepted completion and dedicated cleanup cases also pass.

`scheduler-continuations-native-v3` passes 4/4 build steps and 107/107 cases
(98 scheduler and nine bounded admission). V1 records a helper-name compilation
conflict; V2 passes 106 cases; V3 adds reserved-child discovery. The prepared-memory
build on the same inputs reused its unaffected cached binary. Both binaries were
then directly executed, and the verifier matched all 107 and ten exact names to
source declarations, including the scheduler's diagnostic-output case. All
4,685 native/schema input hashes match both producer receipts. The initial
case-log parser expected single-line diagnostics and rejected that successful
multi-line case; it now requires a terminal OK for every named case and the exact
source-derived inventory. No test failure was hidden or relaxed.
