barriers and the broader original 731-line audit remain incomplete. No pending
start-resource callback has been enabled under the CPU lock. Full heavyweight
qualification remains waived, and no full production-image/default-load claim is
made by these local tests. The original goal remains active.


### Native joint CPU, memory and dense-bandwidth grants (October 16)

The native owning scheduler now accepts a trusted `GrantResources` participant.
Preparation happens outside the scheduler lock. A probe retains no capacity;
actual acquisition runs only after the candidate fits the CPU lane and has paid
its class credit. It commits the complete incremental non-CPU bundle or nothing,
then CPU publication has no fallible resource work left. Callbacks use bounded
try-lock accounting and cannot allocate, wait, perform I/O, reclaim, or reenter
the scheduler. Probe results are cached per dispatch, and an unsuccessful
acquisition marks the candidate waiting for that dispatch, preventing repeated
attempts through deficit rounds. Control roots cannot carry pending foreground
resource requirements.

`PreparedDenseBundle` combines the existing memory identity and dense-search
bandwidth budget. Its lock order is scheduler -> dense-bandwidth admission ->
local memory -> ancestor memory. It honors queued legacy bandwidth waiters.
Memory/ancestor admission is the last fallible action; only then does it charge
bandwidth and transfer both leases to one stable caller-owned adapter. Thus an
I/O refusal never reserves memory, and a memory refusal never charges bandwidth
or CPU. Dense bandwidth preserves its existing semantics: oversized estimates
consume the whole budget, zero estimates consume the minimum unit, and a zero
capacity disables this particular bandwidth gate. This is dense scan bandwidth,
not proof of every physical I/O/fanout owner in the full design.

A local probe can disprove fit. One parent's local snapshot cannot prove fit
through an arbitrary ancestor chain, so parent-backed probes return `unknown`.
Unknown permits an atomic acquisition attempt once CPU fits, but cannot justify
blocking resource-owning continuations behind a CPU assembly barrier. Resource
barriers prevent new starts from stealing the required capacity while allowing
continuations to retire ownership. Competing barriers retain the oldest enqueue
sequence. A paid general team's bounded-read progress path now also checks both
bounded candidate windows; a resource-blocked bounded head cannot hide a retained
continuation. Both paths keep the existing shared query/class credit. General
measured-service accounting and the explicit age backstop remain incomplete.

`Execution.startWithResources` requires a native scheduler, with no unscheduled
fallback. Incremental `requestResources` attaches prepared requirements only at
parked boundaries, preserving the operation, deadline, cancellation and metadata
reservation. Opaque borrowed executors reject this new capability rather than
silently bypassing it. The existing public runtime ABI has not acquired a bundle
forwarding contract. Resource wait polling uses the original queue/deadline clock;
physical retirement may also notify the scheduler after all owner locks release.
Physical cleanup activation discards pending foreground requirements and retains
its dedicated finite authority after close.

CPU park, cancellation and owning CPU finish do not refund the bundle's physical
leases. The caller joins all physical users before `deinitAfterJoin`. The strict
memory identity also fences the bandwidth refund, so a stale copied bundle cannot
consume another scan's credit. Repeated teardown on the same token is idempotent;
a stale identity records an accounting error and leaves the peer's capacity intact.
These are ownership/accounting contracts; they do not establish that every
production buffer or asynchronous I/O user already performs the required joins.

Current evidence: `runnable-resource-bundle-native-v6` passes 26/26 build steps,
with 107 scheduler/admission and 16 joint/bandwidth tests executed; the ten
unaffected prepared-memory tests were cached by the build. All three binaries
were subsequently executed directly, and their exact source-derived inventories
matched all 133 passing names. The receipt/verifier binds 4,687 current
native/schema inputs, binary/log hashes, five deterministic source snapshots and
the unchanged original 731-line design archive. The joint inventory includes
thirteen new contracts and three existing real bandwidth FIFO/cancellation/race
contracts. New coverage includes allocation refusal after preparation, CPU
assembly without partial reservation, local/shared-ancestor/IO denial, retained
leases across CPU parking/finish, incremental acquisition through the real
Execution capsule, original queue timeout and cancellation, retry after a real
thread retires a bandwidth lease without a new submission, cleanup after close,
stale-copy retirement, independent protected progress, and isolated competing
barriers with service debt.

Earlier receipts retain the failures that drove corrections: V1 expected the
wrong existing cancellation spelling; V3 exposed a new wrapper incorrectly
requiring running CPU for a parked resource request; V5 exposed the remaining
head-only bounded progress path. V6 fixes those paths without relaxing authority,
wait limits or accounting. V2 and V4 are intermediate passing inventories before
the additional regressions. Artifacts are under the cumulative integration
receipt directory as `runnable-resource-bundle-native-v6.*`, the core/joint/memory
`*-cases.log` files, `runnable-resource-bundle-verified.json`, producer/verifier
scripts and `runnable-resource-bundle-source-snapshots.json`/gzip files. Older
whole-tree receipts are historical after these native source changes.

The component is implemented and verified locally on macOS ReleaseSafe. Existing
production search/inference/SQL/HTTP/pgwire operator paths have not been switched
to the new bundle adapter. In particular, consuming reserved memory credit in
the actual allocator/buffer owner, forwarding through opaque execution owners,
measured class service, age barriers, additional I/O/fanout profiles and physical
retirement qualification must precede a broader default rollout. Current linked
production images, Linux, overload profiles, recovery/durable ownership and the
remaining rows of the full-design audit are not closed by these tests. Full
heavyweight qualification remains waived; the original full goal remains active.


### Bundle-backed physical allocation consumption (October 17)

`runnable_dense_bundle.Bundle` now exposes stable `AllocationView` instances.
They consume the already-granted slice credit without reserving from the manager
again. All views/workers share the bundle's fixed per-slice counters; an ungranted
slice cannot borrow another slice's capacity, and growth cannot silently expand
the bundle. The physical backing allocator must not independently charge the
same payload again. These counters account requested allocation bytes; allocator
metadata, retained backing pages and whole-process residency remain backing/node
accounting and qualification responsibilities.

Allocation registers its bytes and live-buffer count before invoking the backing
allocator. Backing failure rolls both back. In-place resize admits its delta
before growth and returns it on refusal; shrink and free reduce counters only
after the backing operation. Opaque moving remap is declined so ordinary realloc
allocates/copies/frees with both old and new allocations counted simultaneously.
No backing callback or resource-manager callback runs under the quota mutex.
Capacity versus backing failure is observable per allocator view.

The owner is pinned to its address when a view or resource port is first
published. A copied owner cannot lend another copy of the quota or retire the
original owner's leases; rejected copied teardown records an accounting error
without returning peer capacity. Views also capture manager and reservation
identity, so a view from an earlier request cannot spend credit after the same
bundle storage is reused for another request. Caller-owned bundles and views must
still remain stable through all their physical borrows, and any pending executor
participant must be stopped/detached before its context is retired.

Retirement fences new allocations, allows existing frees/shrinks to finish,
and refuses to release memory or bandwidth while any allocation remains live.
It also counts backing allocations still in flight. If a new backing allocation
completes after the closing fence, the allocator physically frees it before
returning credit and reports refusal instead of publishing its pointer. Once all
physical users join, retrying retirement returns the original strict leases;
normal repeated retirement is idempotent. The non-throwing joined destructor
fails closed on a live-buffer/retiring misuse. Copied-owner teardown is rejected
and consumed without refunding the original owner.

Six new contracts allocate actual buffers through the normal native Execution
capsule and this allocator. They verify shared multi-view and cross-slice limits,
zero backing calls before a grant/on quota refusal, exact node/parent charging at
a hard limit with no second reservation, credit retained through CPU parking and
finish, live-buffer retirement refusal, failed backing allocation and resize
rollback, shrink/free during closing, and old-plus-new realloc peaks with preserved
contents. A backing observer verifies admission precedes physical allocation and
credit remains charged while free executes. Additional cases reject copied-owner
allocation/retirement and stale views after request-storage reuse. A deterministic
threaded case pauses inside the backing allocator, closes the CPU owner, refuses
retirement, queues a competing resource request, completes/frees the unpublished
allocation, and admits the competitor only after final physical retirement. Test
error paths also join that thread and free any retained buffers.

`runnable-bundle-allocator-native-v4` passes 26/26 build steps and all 22 joint
contracts (19 bundle/barrier/allocator cases and three existing bandwidth cases).
The 107 scheduler/admission and ten prepared-memory cases were cached in that
build and then rerun directly along with the joint binary: all 139 exact named
cases pass. The verifier binds 4,687 current native/schema inputs, binary and
case-log hashes, two deterministic source snapshots and the unchanged original
731-line design archive. V1 verifies the first four physical allocator contracts;
V2 adds reuse/in-flight lifetime checks; V3 adds the competing requester; V4
fences allocation publication after close. Native inputs were held unchanged
through each complete helper and direct run. These are local macOS ReleaseSafe
component results, not Linux or current linked production-image qualification.

Evidence in the cumulative integration receipt directory:
`runnable-bundle-allocator-native-v4.json/.log`,
`runnable-bundle-allocator-{core,joint,memory}-cases.log`,
`runnable-bundle-allocator-verified.json`, the verifier script and
`runnable-bundle-allocator-source-snapshots.json`/gzip files. The same bounded
three-target producer was reused. Earlier whole-tree receipts are historical
after the allocator and test-root source changes.

Production operators have not yet been switched to the bundle. HBC search scratch
and immutable generations can outlive a request, so their existing cache ownership
cannot be reassigned to an operation without explicit lifetime/credit transfers.
Each operator must provide the correct physical backing allocator, include bundle
and view metadata in its original bounded admission, and retain these objects
through all physical users. Opaque-owner resource forwarding, production operator
wiring, other resource/IO families, measured general service, age barriers and the
other rows of the original full-design audit remain incomplete. Full heavyweight
qualification stays waived; the full original goal remains active.


### Opaque owner resource forwarding (October 17)

Runnable ABI 15 adds a checked version-1 `ResourceBundle` descriptor, an optional
initial `Start.resources`, and optional `Owner`/`Borrowed.request_resources`
callbacks. The descriptor contains a borrowed physical-owner context and two
integer-result accounting callbacks. API owners copy those three values into the
native scheduler entry before queuing; they retain no pointer to the caller's
transient descriptor frame. The context and every physical resource still require
their original stable lifetime through owning finish and actual joins.

Native grant callbacks now return checked C integers. Unknown probe/acquire values
become `ResourceAccountingMismatch` before any CPU publication. Its append-only
runtime-error detail preserves that cause with internal, non-retryable behavior;
a forged retryable code with the same detail is rejected. No existing detail ID
or status layout changed. Runnable ABI 14 callback tables and short Start/owner/
borrowed/descriptor prefixes are rejected before appended fields, callbacks or IO
borrows are accessed. Protected control/cleanup starts reject resource requirements
before dereferencing even the resource descriptor.

The actual API owner supports both initial and parked incremental bundles. The
checked `Owner.startWithResources` requires the advertised resource capability so
a CPU-only owner cannot silently drop the new Start field. A header-checked
bridge copies resource callbacks between native and ABI participants without heap
allocation or wrapper-owned callback state. Native borrowed executors forward
through that capability under the original lifetime fence. API-local read roots
and physical child receivers expose the same parked attachment path; existing
read policy prechecks and post-grant validation remain mandatory. A second pending
request fails before changing the first callback snapshot.

Reserved children may attach a prepared minimum bundle while still parked before
their first CPU activation. This attaches no CPU or working-set grant: actual
activation still performs the inherited original-authority and joint-resource
checks. Parked attachment preserves the original operation count, retained bytes,
class/deadline/cancellation and parent ownership. Missing capability returns
UnsupportedOperation without creating a new admission, and a closed original
owner remains SchedulerClosed ahead of that optional-capability refusal. Retained
completion/control restrictions still apply. A bridge's finish retires its adapter
or owned child; it cannot finish the original ingress-owned root.

The API owner-port retrieval already passes an explicit output TypeContract and
validates it before writing the Owner value. Its enclosing CallContext/function
signatures are unchanged; no enclosing API/host/storage ABI layout bump is needed.
Inference and storage execution references use separately checked pointers to
Owner/Borrowed rather than embedding the changed table in those public C contexts.
The public runnable prefix is the changed contract and is now 15. These are
process-local callbacks, not a serialized cross-process or remote resource protocol.

Eight new round-trip contracts exercise real API owners, native bridges, local
read adapters and child receivers with the actual memory/bandwidth bundle and
physical allocation view. They verify initial plus incremental credit, frame
poisoning after attachment, refusal to replace pending context, child attachment
before activation, root-versus-bridge finish ownership, live buffers retained after
CPU finish, missing capability and original shutdown authority, invalid integer
results, old/short ABI prefixes and protected pointer ordering. The local-read
case checks both a retained policy refusal before attachment and full validation
after a successful grant. Existing native child lifetime, checked reentry, CPU
loan, inference handoff and error/IO ABI contracts also pass.

107 scheduler/admission, 22 joint/bandwidth/allocator, ten prepared memory, eight

owner/inference handoff cases. The handoff binary repeats existing child/borrow

## SQL numeric fixed scratch and original CPU reentry (2026-10-17)

The production SQL Adapter now supplies an optional scratch source to both its
coordinator scope and the coordinator view of its parallel scope. Eligible numeric
programs prepare bounded participant metadata before parking the existing root.
At the paid, CPU-fitting dispatch, one bounded partition CAS and one bounded node
attempt select either the fixed scratch allocation or the serial alternative
which needs no incremental scratch. Neither alternative creates a new root,
refreshes the deadline, borrows CPU, or consumes dense-search I/O bandwidth.

The fixed allocation uses the partition's physical backing directly, consuming
its existing credit rather than charging the ordinary accountant a second time.
The ordinary bounded allocator continues to own participant metadata and any
preparation/coercion allocations. Scratch is freed before its credit is released;
metadata is freed after the scheduler detaches its callbacks. The synchronous
native transition detaches on every reentry return, including refusal while the
original root remains retained for cleanup. Control and retained phases are
rejected before parking. Borrowed owners need an explicit detachable capability
before using this temporary-stage API; their existing long-lived bundle contract
is unchanged.

The queue restriction checks request lifetime without calling a running-CPU
checkpoint. Full original read-policy validation runs immediately after CPU
reentry and before arithmetic. Eligibility is checked before acquisition; lazy
and unsupported expressions retain existing paths. Scratch pressure, missing
nonblocking accounting, participant allocation failure, and scratch backing OOM
retain serial fallback. Arithmetic, cancellation and deadline errors still
propagate. The production node callback caches the checked linked-storage memory
parent during setup, so dispatch does not perform context lookup or reclaim.
Direct storage uses its existing bounded external reservation method. The API
configuration callback layout changes, requiring API control ABI **49**; the
runnable ABI remains 15, inference-host 38, local inference 4 and storage 100.

`sql-scratch-bundle-native-v4` passes all 78 build steps, including production API
owner exports and the DataServer bounded accounting callback semantic check.
All five actual test binaries were rerun directly: 108 scheduler/admission, four
allocation-budget, 22 SQL kernel/coordinator, 22 joint resource and two production
SQL owner cases. The new owner case exercises ten outcomes: successful scratch,
node busy/denied/unsupported, cancellation/expiry after reservation, participant
OOM, scratch backing OOM, partition exhaustion, and a missing bounded callback.
It checks exact peak charges, physical allocation/free equality, original root,
bytes/deadline, zero child publication and callback detachment after refusal.
Five API 49 layout/prefix cases also pass. This is **163 executions: 158 explicitly
named cases and five anonymous import checks**, all unique case identifiers.
`sql-scratch-bundle-verified.json` independently verifies the source-derived case
inventories, binary/log/runner hashes, nine source snapshots, all 4,690 current
native/schema inputs and the unchanged original 731-line design.

The first integration run exposed a running-CPU checkpoint used while parked;
the queue restriction was corrected before the passing run. A later test expected
zero peak for failed participant backing allocation; accounting correctly charges
before physical allocation and rolls back on failure, so the test now checks that
transient metadata peak and zero final usage. Failed runs remain historical.

This integrates the fixed numeric coordinator buffer only. It does not qualify
all SQL preparation/result allocations, HBC's buffers retained across operations,
other operators/frontends, distributed physical retirement, durable recovery,
measured service/age policy, adaptive sizing or production default-load behavior.
The full original design remains active. Heavyweight full qualification remains
waived, and no new branch, commit, push or PR is created for this work.

## Scheduler age protection and paid continuation drains (2026-10-17)

A blocked ordinary head now becomes an admission barrier on either its configured
bypass count or its original-clock queue age. The age threshold is derived from
the existing wait policy: the lesser of 25 ms and one quarter of `max_wait_ms`.
Each real enqueue starts its queue-age interval. Resource probes, notifications
and polling preserve that timestamp and the original operation deadline. Fitting
heads continue through weighted deficit selection; enqueue sequence orders
competing barriers across independently based request clocks.

The stable owning waiter calls `pollWait` from the existing bounded wait loop.
It validates original authority and observes the request clock outside the owner
lock, then records age protection under that lock. Dispatch reads the recorded
flag. Host clock callbacks therefore cannot reenter a locked scheduler. Direct
asynchronous callers which own an entry can use the same poll method while it is
queued. The existing five-millisecond wait poll observes age without new tasks,
registries, deadlines or timers; CPU/resource retirement still wakes dispatch.

All direct large-admission paths now spend their class deficit. While a paid team
assembles CPU capacity, its normal deficit round remains open and its earned
admission credit remains reserved. A separate bounded selection cursor schedules
retained continuations through the same class-credit ledger, including measured
read debt. The other protected read partition retains its floor. This preserves
weighted team service while physical owners can resume, free memory/I/O buffers
and retire resources. The selection stops promptly when no eligible continuation
exists and retains the independent bounded start/continuation windows. No partial
resource bundle is held by a waiting barrier. Debt is repaid when the barrier can
run, before granting its CPU lease.

`scheduler-age-native-v7` passes all 81 build steps, including the production API
owner and DataServer boundary analysis checks. Every selected binary was rerun
against frozen inputs: 114 scheduler/admission cases, four allocation-budget,
22 SQL kernel/coordinator, 23 joint-resource, two production SQL owner and eight
native-owner forwarding cases. These are **173 executions with 173 unique case
identifiers: 168 explicitly named cases and five anonymous import checks**.
`scheduler-age-verified.json` checks exact source-derived inventories, binary,
runner and log hashes, ten source snapshots, all 4,690 current native/schema
inputs and the unchanged original 731-line design identity.

New contracts cover sparse traffic reaching the age threshold below the bypass
limit; retained owner, health and cleanup progress; competing barriers on unrelated
clock origins; cancellation/expiry with retained ownership; weighted continuation
shares and preservation of paid team credit; maximum read-debt repayment; host
clock observation outside locks; and a real physical buffer with memory plus I/O
credit retained through continuation retirement. Existing mixed-team fairness,
CPU loans, demotion, bounded lookahead, joint bundles and production numeric
scratch contracts pass on the final inputs.

The first broad drain implementation lost earned team service and affected CPU
borrowing. Preserving the paid round and using a bounded progress cursor corrects
those regressions. The final clock review moved observation out of dispatch and
added the lock-detecting clock contract before the final passing run. Earlier
candidate receipts remain historical. Configuration and C ABI layouts are
unchanged by this policy; API 49, runnable 15, native 8, inference-host 38, local
inference 4 and storage 100 remain current.

Age protection controls admission ordering while existing work returns execution
capacity. General-class estimated/measured service reconciliation, complete
operator/resource ownership, production fairness/default profiles, runtime
adaptive sizing and the rest of the original distributed/durable/Cloud design
remain open. Heavyweight full qualification remains waived. This work stays
uncommitted on the existing branch and PR.

## Native measured CPU-lease service reconciliation (2026-10-17)

Managed executions now reconcile their bounded one-quantum-per-slot estimate
against observed active lease slot-time. A successful wait acknowledges the
start of execution; queue residence, wake latency and parked time are excluded.
Every ordinary CPU-return path settles its original class, including yield,
park, team growth, refusal, finish and phase transfer. Shrinking a running team
samples the old width before changing slots, preserving one estimate for the
continuous grant. Live CPU loans keep their original class charge. Foreground
observations settle before switching to independent completion/cleanup clocks.
All clock calls remain outside the scheduler mutex.

A fixed six-class signed ledger keeps fractional rebates and excess-work debt
across roots and class changes. Returning unused estimates can replenish the
same open deficit round, including short cooperative yields. Future eligible
ordinary work repays overrun debt from its class credits. Corrections are bounded
to 64 configured quanta, credits retain their existing cap, and counters saturate.
Clipping is counted. A zero, backwards or unacknowledged sample conservatively
keeps the estimate. A repeated owning finish never calls a retired clock receiver
or settles a charge twice.

The paid-team progress pass repays class debt only above the team's reserved
credit floor. The direct barrier path preserves that reservation until its CPU
bundle fits. Bounded retained-completion/cleanup receivers preserve their prior
class scheduling behavior while present in the discovery window; protected
health and cleanup CPU remains independent. Demotable bounded reads retain their
existing measured transition debt, avoiding a second charge for that same work.
After demotion, subsequent ordinary grants use the general class ledger.

Native `serviceStats()` exposes per-class estimated, observed and unobserved
slot-time, refunds, debt payment, clipping and pending signed correction. These
are execution-lease observations; they are not thread CPU utilization or billing
measurements. Projection through opaque owners and production metrics remains
required before a runtime adaptive controller can use them.

kernel/coordinator, 23 joint-resource, two production SQL owner and eight native
forwarding cases. This is **182 executions with 182 unique case identifiers: 177
explicitly named cases and five anonymous import checks**. Independent verifier
`measured-service-verified.json` binds exact source-derived inventories, binary,
runner and log hashes, ten source snapshots, all 4,690 native/schema inputs and
the unchanged original 731-line design identity.

Nine new contracts verify debt surviving root retirement; fractional refunds and
park exclusion; 2:1 measured slot-time shares with quarter-quantum and four-quantum
requests, both as fresh roots and indefinitely yielding continuations; team
resize accounting; origin class and CPU loans; protected completion on a different
clock; extreme/zero/backwards/unobserved clocks and repeated finish; short-yield
refunds; and preservation of paid team credit during an overrunning continuation.
The SQL publication fixture now uses controlled actual quantum exhaustion and
checks observed service before peer progress. Checkpoint count alone cannot
establish that a small real-time kernel exhausted its measured share. An earlier
candidate's minimum yield charge was removed to preserve measured fairness for
cheap cooperative operators; current short-yield and continuation-share tests
verify that policy directly.

Private native entry/owner metadata now contains fixed-size service observations
and ledgers. C ABI and configuration layouts are unchanged: API 49, runnable 15,

The implementation is uncommitted in the existing worktree/branch/PR. Full

The full heavyweight qualification sweep remains waived.

## Versioned API service telemetry and metrics (2026-10-17)

The existing scheduler snapshot now carries version-1 service telemetry through
API ABI **50**. Policy, live ownership, counters and signed service correction
are copied under one scheduler lock. The projection converts native signed
correction into separate unsigned debt and rebate gauges in the fixed class
order: query general, write, inference, background, query bounded and query
analytical. The C payload owns its version, size, measurement model and explicit
availability flag. No native pointers or compiler-specific signed integers cross
the boundary.

The checked opaque getter validates the API function-table prefix before fetching
the callback, then uses the existing checked call/output contract and validates
the service payload before returning it. API 49 contexts and old output contracts
are refused before owner dereference or output writes. The enclosing workload
stats layout also changes, so API 50 is required for both telemetry and handler
workload snapshots. Runnable 15, native 8, inference-host 38, local inference 4,
storage 100 and worker wire 13 remain unchanged.

The production metric renderer exports availability plus the service quantum,
six counter families (estimated, observed, unobserved, refunded, debt repaid and
clipped adjustments), and pending debt/rebate gauges. Every per-class family has
six server-owned labels. An unavailable owner emits `service_available 0` and
omits service usage families; it cannot fabricate zero observed usage. Bad
versions, short service layouts, unknown measurement models, invalid quanta or
contradictory/out-of-bounds corrections fail before rendering this snapshot.
Availability means the observation format is supported; phase coverage still
requires checking unobserved and clipping signals and the owner inventory.

### TypeScript unread response failure retires admission (2026-10-17)

The TypeScript SDK retained a request slot when fetch aborted or otherwise
failed an unread response after returning headers: only a later wrapper pull or
explicit body cancellation observed the error. `RequestAdmission.fetch` now
observes the upstream reader's terminal rejection and errors the wrapper and
releases its idempotent lease. Successful reader closure is deliberately not a
retirement signal: explicit cancellation may resolve pending reads before its
physical cancellation promise settles. That path still owns retirement until
its promise completes.

A deterministic unread-source-error regression failed before the fix because
the queued request never dispatched, then passed afterward. A second regression
uses native fetch and a real localhost HTTP listener: aborting an unread body
admits the waiting request before the first body is consumed or explicitly
canceled. All 28 admission cases pass, including the existing pending-read versus
physical-cancel race, early NDJSON/generator exit, queue cancellation/FIFO,
shared database/inference routes and close behavior. Type checking and targeted

`sdk-ts-unread-error-verified.json` in the cumulative integration directory.

unblocks transports that await cancellation while keeping admission capacity
charged until physical close returns. Concurrent closes join the same once;
the caller's parent context and original close/operation errors are preserved.

### Embedded model and buffer admission — 2026-10-17

### CUDA cache buffer admission and physical retirement — 2026-10-17

ModelManager's canonical prompt-cache factory now owns a device-budget capability
from its existing shared resource domain. Each buffer credit independently
retains that domain and an exact GPU KV AdmissionLease. Credit records use the
cache's allocator, so parented/supervised host bookkeeping is admitted too.
Closing the cache drops its capability after storage/manager teardown; outstanding
buffer credits keep the domain and external parent capability alive independently.

CUDA cache K/V and block-table allocations reserve the full requested new buffer
size before calling the existing context-local allocator/driver. Old buffers
remain charged during growth. Driver/context/local-limit failures roll back the
new credit. Full allocation descriptors carry credits through deferred retirement,
independent of logical view length. Successful cuMemFree releases the credit;
failed context switches or frees preserve the descriptor and charge for retry.
The deferred queue compacts failed entries instead of dropping them. Credited
KV buffers bypass generic scratch reuse so that cached scratch cannot strand KV
credits; existing stream-completion handling governs deferred physical frees.
CUDA logical cache observations are suppressed where this physical factory
budget and admitted host allocator are present. Metal retains its observation.

## 2026-10-17 zero-byte admission lease ownership

zero-byte admission, peak-to-zero reduction and provisional owner callbacks all

usage as its exclusion condition, allowing the token's original context to be
detached before retirement. The controller now tracks a checked independent live
lease count. It publishes that count before external reservation, unwinds it on
refusal, and retires it only after the external release callback returns.

and controller teardown remain fenced until all leases retire, including local
zero-byte leases. The steady path adds no allocation or callback under the
admission ledger lock. No external ABI or resource limit changed.

### Shared identity table storage and bounded retirement

Reservation, prepared/active batch, and observer identity tables now admit their
backing allocation requests through the common manager and every installed
memory parent. A finite 64 MiB default cap applies to their combined storage even
when the aggregate budget is unlimited. These bytes also consume the existing
aggregate envelope; the cap adds no extra physical quota. Growth admits the
complete new table while the old table remains charged, and removing logical
identities leaves retained table storage charged until physical free. Manager
snapshots distinguish active table bytes, the cap, and retirement debt.

The allocator context exists only for each unmanaged-map operation, so startup
moves retain no allocator pointer into a former manager address. Late parent
installation includes existing startup charges. Single, oversized, batch, and
partial reservation paths preserve metadata admission when committing payload
usage. Partial fallback computes available payload after table admission.
Checked payload retirement guards the table/debt floor. Checked batch admission
continues to distinguish backing allocator OOM from a quota refusal.

Bounded rollback and rehash retirement originally invoked the legacy parent
release callback. Three regressions reproduced that behavior and bypass of a busy
parent's non-waiting refusal. Bounded retirement now uses only the non-waiting release port.
After physical free, an unavailable parent leaves exact credit debt in fixed
manager storage. New metadata allocation first settles existing debt, and the
independent payload-retirement consumer can settle it under its original cleanup
checkpoint even when no payload registry entry remains. Ordinary teardown settles
remaining debt before closing the parent. The unchanged three failing cases pass
after the fix. Two earlier regressions similarly establish actual prepared-table
charging and refusal before backing allocation/publication. An initial empty
filtered run and later fixture/compile corrections are explicitly excluded from
product red/green evidence.

### Shared standalone control-object admission and spare-cache recovery

Standalone lease records now join the common metadata byte cap before backing
allocation, including records not yet published as tokens. Active-lease and
prompt/tokenizer wrapper maps use the same admission path as their backing
storage grows. Cached spare records and retained map capacity remain charged;
removing a logical token or observer does not return still-retained storage.
Identity tables and these control objects compete for the same existing 64 MiB
cap and aggregate/parent envelope. Their combined growth peak cannot bypass
admission. Table bytes and provisional/retained control-object bytes remain
separate in snapshots, since a prepared request's permanent table floor must not
include control objects another owner can retire.

The operation-local allocator context preserves typed quota refusal separately
from backing OOM. Its backing allocator runs outside the accounting mutex, with
credit held before allocation and through physical free. Unmanaged containers
retain no pointer to the stack context; freeing after startup relocation uses a
fresh context at the current manager address. Closing a manager with live control
objects is rejected. Callers supply a raw lifetime backing allocator rather than
an allocator already charging this manager or an ancestor. Standalone admission
also uses checked batch reservation so identity-table backing OOM survives the
public status conversion without publishing a token.

The lease pool now keeps at most 64 spare records and destroys excess records
outside its pool mutex. This is an additional idle-cache limit; all active,
provisional, cached and map storage still shares the byte cap. An 80-record burst
regression fills a real aggregate envelope and proves recycling returns physical
capacity for subsequent work. A controlled unlimited-cache variant fails that
unchanged test, while the restored bounded implementation passes. This avoids
retaining a concurrency burst's entire record pool until service shutdown.

Three initial regressions reproduced missing provisional/cached charges, cap
bypass before record allocation, and missing wrapper-map storage. Their unchanged
test bodies pass with the shared allocator. The additional checks cover real
concurrent provisional allocation, common admission before backing callbacks,
physical-free ordering, object/table cap competition in both directions, typed
OOM/parent refusal, wrapper old/new-table overlap and refusal atomicity, and
startup relocation followed by repeated late parent installation. Legitimate
wrapper metadata pressure is refused without reporting accounting corruption.
Synthetic payload-only fixtures explicitly provision/count their own actual
metadata before publishing work; raw allocation-failure tests retain their
specific failure paths.

### Private API cleanup memory inside the existing process reserve

The API's existing prepaid control budget now has separate ordinary-control and
cleanup partitions. Cleanup receives `control_bytes / 2`; ordinary controls retain
the remainder, where `control_bytes = min(16 MiB, request_memory_bytes / 8)`.
The original foreground/read allocation and total process control/transport pin
remain unchanged. Cleanup allocations do not take a second charge against the
node. Both partitions must physically retire before the API releases that pin.

Resource-manager cleanup, read-retirement and reconciliation runtime heaps use
the private partition. Imported cleanup-worker receivers and shared control/cleanup
lane receivers use it too. Ordinary HTTP/pgwire controls, remote owner state and
per-request endpoint bindings retain their ordinary allocation paths; they cannot
claim this reserve by sending a class hint. Allocation provenance routes resize,
remap and free back to the original partition across allocator views. Public HTTP
budgets exclude cleanup capacity, including API configurations without a scheduler.

Workload memory snapshots expose `cleanup` separately. The existing three-part
kernel ABI aggregates ordinary-control and cleanup statistics into its control
entry; its peak is a conservative sum of partition peaks. The API's private runtime
and receiver floor is implemented, while producer-side worker/IO allocations,
remote journal/owner metadata and other completion/resume paths still need their
own verified minimum-capacity treatment. This is not proof of every control path
progressing under overload, nor completion of the original full design.

### Caller-funded worker producers and preallocated journal publication

The private kernel ABI is now revision 51. Worker acquisition requires a valid
allocator callback table; missing funding and older factory versions fail before
worker publication. The borrower creates a stable allocator carrier before calling
the producer, which copies the C-layout callback table into its owned wrapper.
Moving the returned lease cannot leave an executor referencing a stack allocator.

Exclusive workers allocate their executor and Threaded heap metadata from that
caller funding. `BackendRuntime.WorkerLease` records the actual allocator selected
at creation and releases the executor with it after the physical worker join.
The producer wrapper survives that join, then frees through an independent copy
of the allocator table. The borrower retires its receiver and carrier last. API
resource cleanup, read-retirement and reconciliation use this funded native path;
imported counterparts use the same required allocator contract. Allocation failures
retain `OutOfMemory`, while worker-capacity failures retain their capacity status.

Shared-role borrower wrappers also use their own caller funding. The shared
executor remains node-owned, so releasing its first borrower cannot invalidate a
peer's allocator. A protected node bank for shared executors and their later task
allocations is still required. The SQL completion runtime and its reaper still
use foreground allocation paths and need integration with verified completion
capacity. Neither all bridge-frame/OS-stack accounting nor full control-progress
coverage is claimed by this component.

The journal audit found an existing protection: `remote_fence_store.Store` owns
its floor/destination tables and write buffer at initialization. A new test denies
all subsequent store-allocator allocations, persists a fence while old work is
pending, retires that work, and verifies the durable generation after reopening.
This closes the suspected *store-allocator* publication gap without adding another
reserve. It does not prove all filesystem/executor metadata is protected, or that
late remote-owner bootstrap succeeds under ordinary-control exhaustion.

### Node-owned prepaid SQL executor heaps

Shared SQL worker executors now use a stable node-owned bank when their runtime
is configured with a memory parent. Execution, control, cleanup and bounded-read
roles each have a separate 1 MiB default heap floor. The parent admits all four
floors plus the bank's own metadata before that metadata is allocated. Runtime
configuration can supply different limits, with each executor constructor's
minimum checked before admission. These are initial bounded heap defaults, not a
completed workload/profile qualification or a bound on OS thread-stack mappings.

`BackendRuntime` owns the bank, rather than the first API borrower. Its actual
`Io.Threaded` objects and allocations through their allocator, including future
metadata, spend the appropriate role floor. There is no foreground-allocator
fallback after a configured floor is exhausted. Backing allocation failure rolls
back local usage; physical free precedes returning local credit. Reallocation
fallback admits the old+new allocation peak. The parent's prepaid charge remains
held through all executor lifetimes, and bank metadata physically frees before
that charge returns. Runtimes without a configured parent retain their existing
injected allocator contract; accounting for all other node/runtime construction
metadata remains separate work.

A separate shared-SQL lifetime gate fences both capability acquisition and late
bank installation. Installation after a shared capability attempt is refused.
`closeSharedSqlMemory` closes only shared SQL admission, waits through borrowers,
physical worker joins and final pool bookkeeping, then destroys the bank. Its
snapshot accessor and concurrent close serialize metadata access. Other runtime
lanes remain available for storage-context shutdown; normal runtime destruction
also closes this child before destroying general I/O. Shutdown refusals preserve
the role's rejection counter.

Standalone startup supplies its existing early process parent. Clustered data
startup installs the compiled storage parent's bank before publishing consumers,
then explicitly closes this memory child before destroying that storage context.
Legacy data startup creates an early process root, funds the bank from it and
joins provisioned storage to the same root, avoiding separate aggregate ceilings.
A new semantic check analyzes the actual standalone and data entrypoints in both
compiled-storage and legacy profiles, without linking provider archives or
executing those entrypoints.

That check exposed and fixed three existing integration gaps: data read-memory
metrics now use the existing opaque handler snapshot (no ABI extension), the
standalone catalog explicitly refuses the distributed remote-initialization call
alongside its unsupported enrollment calls, and controlled Lite publication
mutexes use the bounded lock helper's `tryLock`/`unlock` contract with the original
wait authority and post-acquisition cancellation rollback.

### Physical worker termination before capacity retirement

Continuing the stack-ownership audit found a prerequisite lifetime defect in the
pinned Zig `std.Io.Threaded`: its four spawn paths detach workers, while deinit
waits for worker bodies through a wait group. A worker finishes that group before
pthread TLS destructors run. Consequently the previous runtime could return a
worker slot, its heap funding and producer ownership while a physical thread was
still retiring. A blocked TLS-destructor regression demonstrates this on the old
backend (`physical-worker-retirement-red-v2`, actual exit 1); its exact test body
is unchanged in the final passing run.

`tools/prepare_joinable_threaded.py` now generates a build-cache-local standard
library overlay from the pinned toolchain. It rejects an unknown source layout
before writing output and leaves the installed/Nix compiler library unchanged.
The overlay adds an opt-in join policy: finite limits at most 256, a bounded
retained-handle array, and actual `Thread.join` calls after worker-body draining.
All four spawn paths retain their handles. Closing prevents new concurrent/group
concurrent work and runs async/group async submissions inline. Exiting opted-in
workers clear the standard library's worker TLS pointer before TLS destructors.
Default detached join policy remains unchanged for other users of Threaded.

Both BackendRuntime-owned executor constructors opt in through
`initOwnedThreaded`; stock-library builds fail with an actionable composition
error. Root and embedded build graphs apply the generated library to consumers
and module-linked archives. Public Zig consumers must inherit the library path
and its generation dependency from the `antfly-lite` artifact; the embedded README
and fetched consumer fixture show this. Python 3 is required for generation, with
copy fallback when resource symlinks are unavailable. Private kernel ABI **52**
rejects older worker factories rather than accepting their weaker retirement
promise. Public C/SDK ABI and generic runtime-native ABI are unchanged.

The fetched Apache source package now carries the generator. Packaging excludes
standalone vendored test roots from initial selection while preserving dependency
closure and strict license checks. Fourteen first-party embedded SPDX headers
were aligned with the repository's existing Apache source-root classification;
vendored notices were not changed. The standalone package also handles Mach-O's
custom shared-library install step without removing the existing `antfly` compile
artifact on other platforms.

existing cumulative-integration receipt directory: **82/82 steps succeed**.
Twenty worker behavior cases and nine declaration cases execute without skips,

### Guarded owned stacks and prepaid SQL stack floors

The next ownership step replaces libc-owned stacks for BackendRuntime-owned
pthread executors with caller-owned page mappings. The generated library now
patches both `std/Io/Threaded.zig` and `std/Thread.zig`; build inputs track both
installed sources, both layouts validate before output is copied, and manifests
record both original and transformed hashes. Installed/Nix library files remain
unchanged. The existing public Zig consumer library-inheritance requirement still
applies; the embedded README explains the stronger native stack ownership.

Each opted-in pthread spawn admits a page-aligned mapping for the requested stack
(minimum 16 KiB, preserving the pinned implementation's existing minimum), rounds
it with checked arithmetic, and includes one inaccessible page at each end.
`pthread_attr_setstack` receives only the payload. The standard Thread entry
wrapper still calls the usual `callFn`, including signal-stack setup, and its
metadata is allocated from the executor's allocator. A rejected attribute or
pthread creation unwinds metadata and mappings. A caller stack too small for the
linked image's TLS produces a resource refusal rather than an unreachable panic.
Overflowing explicit worker stack sizes are rejected before executor allocation.
The default requested stack remains **16 MiB**; it has not been reduced to make
small-memory tests pass.

Threaded retains each mapping with its thread handle and frees it only after
actual `Thread.join`, covering TLS destructors. Stack allocators must provide
exclusive page mappings and unmap without reading protected guard pages. Owned
runtime lanes default to the page allocator, so those mappings have an explicit
unmap owner. Other Threaded users retain the default join/stack policy. Non-pthread
backends retain their platform stack paths and are not qualified by this change.

For parent-backed shared SQL roles, a separate stack segment for each role
precharges the complete configured role ceiling before runtime executor
construction/publication. Execution, control, cleanup and bounded-read stack
floors cannot spend each other's capacity or consume task-heap floors. The exact
mapping size, including both guards, is multiplied by each role's worker ceiling;
all products and sums are checked. Physical mapping failure returns segment
credit. Free unmaps before local credit return, and the full node pin remains
until bank destruction after shared consumers and their physical joins drain.
Stack segments reject non-page lengths and alignments above the runtime page size,
preventing hidden page rounding or transient over-aligned mappings.

With the existing default 32-worker profile, shared roles reserve 26 stacks:
12 execution, five control, eight cleanup and one bounded read. This costs 416 MiB
of requested payload, plus guard pages, the existing four 1 MiB task-heap floors
and bank metadata. An 8 MiB parent is therefore refused before executor
construction. The three existing parent-pressure runtime tests now use a 1 GiB
parent, reserve the full bundle first, and still exhaust the remaining parent;
the generic small-bank tests retain their small limits. Manual/borrowed runtimes
that cannot supply shared workers do not prepay unusable pthread stack capacity.

Three new behavior tests cover undersized-node/overflow refusal before internal
runtime allocation; actual worker stack addresses inside the supplied payload,
inaccessible guards, TLS-blocked physical release, OS-observed whole-range unmap

### One early memory ancestor for host and compiled storage

The remaining-lane audit found that compiled storage creates its own runtime and
resource manager, while the data host previously acquired its SQL memory parent
from that context after host-runtime construction. Charging more host lanes alone
would leave separate process ceilings and a parent whose destruction preceded
some host teardown. Both production standalone and data entrypoints now create a
stable host-owned `node_memory_root` before either storage context or host runtime.
It outlives both. Legacy storage still joins that root; compiled storage receives
a checked, copied parent table at context birth. Host shared SQL banks now borrow
the early root directly, so their parent no longer depends on storage-context
lifetime. These are hierarchical child limits under one ancestor, not two budgets
that can independently spend the process limit.

The private `kernel_runtime_services.Request` advances from version 2 to **3**
and appends an optional memory-parent pointer. Old request prefixes are rejected
before reading the tail. A separate two-word parent-header check rejects old or
truncated parent layouts before copying the table. Neither the request nor the
caller's table needs to survive construction; the parent callback context does.
The storage-owner ABI remains 100 and API kernel ABI remains 52. Public C/SDK
interfaces and generic runtime-native ABI are unchanged.

`BootstrapAllocation` precharges requested context-header bytes before physical
allocation, rolls the charge back on allocation failure, and returns it only
after physical context destruction. The actual provider saves the allocator and
parent before poisoning/freeing its receiver. `PhysicalStorageResources` now has
`initWithBudgetsAndParent`: its temporary manager joins the ancestor before fixed
cache metadata admission and shard allocation. Existing no-parent constructors
retain their allocator-error contract. Failure cleanup releases cache/identity
metadata and header charges in physical-retirement order. Constructor/destructor
bodies of the real exported storage provider are checked by a dedicated semantic
target, including both ordinary and borrowed-I/O construction branches.

Reclamation remains purpose-bound: inference still receives the nearest compiled
storage child's parent port, whose cache hooks can reclaim under ancestor pressure.
It does not bypass those hooks by borrowing the otherwise empty host root's
reclaimer list. Its child forwards accounting and pressure epochs to the same
ancestor. The standalone bootstrap test now distinguishes those callback contexts
while proving that either path competes for the same root capacity. API/storage
parent ports likewise retain their existing child ownership and reclaimer routes.

Process telemetry reads exact memory totals, peaks, limits and counters from the
host root through a host-only borrowed pointer in `DataServerConfig`. Per-owner
slice attribution remains in the merged storage snapshot. All four DataServer
construction paths retain that pointer; standalone/data serving entrypoints pass
the common root, whose lifetime exceeds the server. The root implementation
pointer never crosses the storage ABI. The storage context's own metrics remain
scoped to its resource manager.

Six new live metadata tests cover ancestor refusal before physical cache
allocation, parent-table/request prefix validation and copying, bootstrap-header
allocation failure and physical-free ordering, complete ancestor rollback across
cache-construction allocation failures, global totals/peaks without duplicate
child charges, and relocated resource ownership under sibling pressure. The last
case refuses a new byte while a host sibling holds the remaining root, evicts a
real unpinned cache entry through the storage child's callback, and admits work
before that sibling releases. This verifies the reclaimer route needed by the
shared hierarchy rather than merely comparing counters.

charged identity-table bytes. Assertions now include the live identity/control/

The implementation's existing metadata charges were preserved. No production
accounting was weakened to obtain a passing test.

### Separate service and shared SQL worker reservations

The combined-capacity audit found that default shared SQL roles reserved 26 of
`worker_capacity = 32`, even though that field was documented as the service
worker envelope. Raft senders, snapshots, listeners, apply/progress, maintenance,
reporting and the API reaper also reserve service workers. A representative
composition reserves 16 service slots before shared SQL admission; both classes
could not reliably start together.

`BackendRuntimeLaneLimits.sql_worker_capacity` now declares a separate 32-slot
SQL envelope. Dedicated service admission retains its existing 32-slot envelope.
The default declared profile is 284 under an explicit aggregate ceiling of 288;
individual executors remain capped at 256. This accounts for the additional SQL
envelope without silently shrinking existing lane limits. These are bounded
per-runtime ceilings, not a claim of measured process-wide defaults or proof
that multiple storage/host runtimes already share every physical resource.

Private class counters enforce each envelope. SQL callers cannot select the
service reservation path through their shared-role factory. Both contribute to
the existing total/peak counters; health metrics also expose the separate used
and declared capacities. Physical executor join and stack unmapping precede
reservation release. Aggregate credit is released before class admission reopens,
so a concurrent replacement cannot transiently inflate the total above its sum.

Private API kernel ABI 53 carries both service `capacity` and SQL
`shared_capacity`. Imported request/returned-capacity validation, server pool
sizing and provider publication use the appropriate class. Old ABI prefixes are
rejected before reading the expanded layout. Shared capacity defaults to zero
for factories that only provide exclusive workers. Public C and SDK ABIs are
unchanged.

Regression coverage activates service and all four SQL roles together, through
native and imported receivers, including the full service reservation ceiling.
The existing 32-consumer saturation case now retains all 32 service slots while
foreground/cleanup saturation leaves SQL control and bounded-read progress.
Additional cases check different imported class limits, disabled SQL admission,
failed construction credit rollback and retry, and preservation of protected
workers after failed foreground publication. API rollback tests inject actual
node-allocator failures; the reaper test still exhausts its own service class.

### Node funding for runtime metadata and owned IO stacks

Standard standalone/data startup now supplies the common early process parent
through `BackendRuntime.Config.memory_parent`. The actual compiled storage owner
uses its stable resource manager's port, which forwards to that same process
ancestor when supplied and preserves a local authority for independent contexts.
Both parents outlive runtime destruction and the separately charged handle.

A stable `storage/runtime_memory.Owner` charges its own header before allocation,
wraps runtime heap allocations, and supplies a separate page-only allocator for
owned IO stack mappings. Metadata is charged by requested allocation size;
complete guard/payload mappings are charged before mapping. Failed physical
allocation returns its charge. Freeing and physical joins precede credit return.
Resize/remap use allocation fallback so the old-plus-new peak is admitted.
BackendRuntime's primary durable, lazy API/inference/control/Raft/forwarding
executors and ordinary exclusive worker stacks use this authority. Runtime
registries, executor objects, task frames and maintenance metadata use its heap.

Prepaid SQL banks retain their original backing allocator, avoiding a second
charge for physical allocations already covered by role floors. Caller-funded
exclusive worker metadata also retains its caller authority; its default stack
allocator now uses the node owner. An explicitly supplied stack allocator keeps
its existing authority. The runtime closes borrowers and physically joins owned
IO executors before destroying the stable allocator context. The handle's charge
survives its final physical free. Manual borrowed IO retains its caller lifetime.

Admission is dynamic for these stacks rather than prepaying every possible lazy
worker at startup. Root exhaustion refuses a new mapping without publishing it;
prepaid SQL control/cleanup floors remain independent. This does not establish
new protected floors for every other progress class or qualify complete default
startup compositions under pressure. Metrics publish accounting availability,
tracked runtime heap/mapping bytes and allocation rejection counters; the common
root remains authoritative for process totals.

### Node funding for PDF worker stacks and retained scratch

The PDF affinity lane now receives the runtime's stack and scratch allocation
authorities. On pthread platforms its workers use exact caller-owned mappings
with inaccessible guard pages at both ends, preserving the existing 16 MiB

workers are physically joined before their mappings are released. Failed lane
construction closes the queue, joins workers already started, then frees all

charge complete pages before mapping; unsupported alignment or rounding overflow
fails without allocation. Release recomputes the exact mapping extent and unmaps
before returning root credit. Resize/remap use admitted allocation fallback,
including the physical old-plus-new peak. Arena pages retained between jobs keep
their node charge until arena reset/destruction actually frees them. Scratch
mapping bytes and allocation rejections have separate health metrics. Existing
lane/batch limits still bound logical backing requests; the node additionally
bounds physical page mappings, including rounding.

### Private manual IO and retained native storage ownership

Private manual runtime helpers now accept a memory parent. Their IO executor is
allocated from the stable runtime authority and retained as an auxiliary owned
lane. Runtime teardown keeps that lane alive through registry/borrower teardown,
then physically joins it before destroying its allocator context. The handle
retains its original backing allocator and releases its header charge last.
Legacy helper signatures delegate to the parent-aware constructors.

Default DB open now creates its resource manager before an owned runtime and
supplies that manager's parent port. Cleanup order keeps the manager alive until
runtime destruction. The private externally locked Lite C API path creates the
same automatically sized resource profile before its manual helper, supplies it
to DB open, and transfers ownership into the handle. Close destroys DB/backend,
then the runtime, then that manager. This reuses the existing sizing policy.

`NativeStoragePool` now closes state admission and drains retained state/path-lock
owners before the runtime can release its parent or IO lanes. Each native storage
state copies the configured parent into its own stable funded allocator. Metadata
and owned guarded stack mappings remain charged until the last range, descriptor
or explicit lease is released and the executor physically joins. Closing a native
storage handle still allows an already retained future/lease to finish. Runtime
shutdown waits for those users instead of freeing their accounting context.
Last-release notification is serialized with pool destruction. Path locks retain
an equivalent pool lease and funded IO authority through close and physical join.

`threaded_io_limits.initOwnedService` selects the generated joinable executor,
finite concurrent capacity and bounded CPU-derived async capacity. Both admission
paths use Threaded's shared busy count. Native states join physically even when
no memory parent was configured. The generic process service constructor remains
available for other lifetime owners; this does not claim those owners are funded.

## Restore executor authority and runtime/manager transfer

stable addresses. Moving their public values preserves borrowed std.Io handles.

stacks; managed manager lifetimes survive the public owner's release. Teardown
joins real workers before freeing users or closing descriptors. Bridge payload
maps retain their existing allocator contract; this does not claim that all
bridge data is charged to the executor budget.

backup manifest reads/writes, directory copies and remote-store setup propagate
it rather than opening implicit private pools. Convenience owned preparation
uses bounded, joinable OwnedIo. Connection options forward explicit IO and
resources to both open and create. Portable generation publication preserves the
live file's executor while swapping descriptors, so the disposable generation
borrows that executor and the destination manager through its cleanup.

### Native control executor reserve and metadata scheduler

The funded native BackendRuntime now reserves its control executor's 1 MiB
heap and the entire configured control stack-mapping ceiling before publication.
The default remains eight workers with the unchanged 16 MiB stack payload and
exact guard/mapping overhead. First control-lane construction, futures and worker
metadata use the private heap; guarded mappings use its private stack allocator.
They cannot borrow ordinary node memory. The parent keeps the complete reserve
until physical thread join, TLS destruction and executor teardown. Ordinary
heap/stack statistics still include actual control allocations, using combined
atomic counters rather than adding independent peaks. Separate control reserve,
live/peak and refusal metrics expose this ownership on data and metadata health.
Borrowed and manual IO retain their existing allocator authority.

Metadata CLI now resolves admission once and shares one NodeRunnableOwner
between API and backend/storage consumers. Its default waiting policy matches
the common bounded query policy; fixed, disabled and explicit fail-fast settings
remain authoritative. Consumer shutdown closes admission before joining service
work and destroys the owner only after runtime and storage consumers retire.

while ordinary node memory is completely exhausted, refusal at the private heap
ceiling despite available ordinary memory, recovery after release and retention
of the full reserve through a blocked pthread TLS destructor. Four unrelated
128 MiB fixtures explicitly use a valid one-worker control profile; production
defaults are unchanged. The metadata service test takes a backend runnable grant
and observes it in API statistics, proving one shared controller. Policy override
tests use the production resolver; the actual CLI startup bodies are analyzed in
both storage profiles but are not executed by this suite.

The original design remains incomplete. This reserve covers the control executor,
not every caller buffer, metadata catalog/WAL/media allocation, recovery payload
or Raft transport dependency. NativeDurableJobLane.submit still allocates an
entry, queue growth and a future from ordinary memory. Publication-outbox and
portable-activation recovery can submit after durable obligations exist, so
those paths require pre-admitted completion resources and a dependency inventory.
Registered-owner beginJob and probe rearming are already allocation-free; the
remaining reserve must protect the job and its downstream completion path.
Retired-generation cleanup copies paths and queues work after recording durable
cleanup intent. Runtime restart supervision also allocates a Work payload from
page_allocator;
protecting only lane bookkeeping would miss that payload. Raft inbound/outbound
executors still use ordinary node heap and mapping authority. These are the next
progress-floor gaps, alongside the remaining original-design work. Full
qualification remains waived, and working-tree package evidence is not release
provenance. Work remains uncommitted/unpushed on the canonical branch/worktree/PR.

### Native Raft executor startup floors

A funded native BackendRuntime reserves each Raft direction independently: a
private 1 MiB heap plus the complete configured guarded stack-mapping ceiling.
The production default remains 32 inbound and 32 outbound workers with unchanged
16 MiB stack payloads. Lazy executor headers, futures and worker metadata use the
corresponding private heap; mappings use the matching prepaid stack authority.
Ordinary memory and other protected directions cannot borrow this credit.
The pinned Threaded implementation shares one busy-worker count between async
and concurrent work; the runtime bounds async at or below the concurrent ceiling. The
memory owner retains all three control/Raft reserves through real worker join,
pthread TLS destruction and final physical teardown. Existing aggregate heap/map
metrics include actual Raft allocations, and separate no-label direction metrics
report prepaid ceilings, live/peak bytes and refusals.

Native HttpHost setup now propagates inbound/outbound lane refusal instead of
constructing an independent executor/listener. This also applies when the caller
provides a custom request executor but the transport still needs native outbound
IO. Explicit manual/hybrid compositions retain their existing adapter authority.

The larger default floor is a startup admission requirement: a node must fund the
complete configured lane ceilings before publication. Focused success fixtures
were enlarged to fit this profile, rather than reducing production concurrency
or stack sizes. Four existing 128 MiB non-Raft fixtures explicitly configure one
worker in each Raft direction as well as their existing one-worker control lane.
Those fixtures are not qualification of the 32+32 default under 128 MiB.

New native cases cover simultaneous cold publication of all 64 Raft workers
while ordinary memory is completely exhausted, independent heap refusal/retry,
continued control progress, actual TLS retirement in each direction and refusal
before memory-owner backing allocation. HttpHost tests induce refusal in both
directions with and without a custom executor and check service-lease rollback.

This is executor ownership evidence, not complete Raft progress qualification.
Compiled storage context creation in capi/server_owner.zig also constructs a
separate BackendRuntime under its child resource manager. The current runtime
services port shares the memory parent and runnable owner, not the native
executor lanes or durable-job lane. Full CLI startup therefore needs the sum of
those separately owned floors until a complete execution-services handoff can
share them. Borrowing only general IO would switch that context to manual/inline
durable execution and is not an equivalent replacement. These focused tests do
not execute a compiled CLI/provider startup.
HttpFrameDriver.startAsyncSenders still constructs isolated StdHttpExecutors per
sender; these have independent Threaded pools outside the BackendRuntime Raft

payloads, resolver/provider work, file descriptors and the persistence/apply

client can use page_allocator, another authority gap. Future work must account
for the entire task graph while preserving cancellation isolation and bounded
service capacity; changing only the shared lane does not establish that bound.

The backing-allocator/parent identity issue also remains open: an embedding host
which passes a budgeted backing allocator and the same root as memory_parent can
charge allocations twice. These tests use an independent backing allocator and

Durable completion still needs pre-admission before irreversible decisions.
NativeDurableJobLane entry/queue/future allocations remain ordinary memory;
publication-outbox and portable activation schedule after durable obligations
exist. Registered-owner job admission and probe rearming are allocation-free.
Retired-generation cleanup records durable intent before copying a queued path
payload, and runtime restart and cleanup Work payloads still allocate from page_allocator. Persisted debt loaded at startup also needs a bounded reserved recovery path;
pre-commit tickets alone cannot cover obligations from before this process. A durable
intent preserves retryability but does not prove in-process progress under full
memory exhaustion. The original design remains incomplete, with full
qualification waived. Work remains on the canonical branch/worktree/PR,
uncommitted and unpushed.

### Node execution services shared with compiled storage (2026-10-18)

Standalone, data and metadata startup now create the node execution runtime
before the compiled storage context and pass its checked execution offer into
that context. The storage runtime owns local policy/storage metadata and a
retained execution scope, rather than another set of native execution pools,
control/Raft reservations or SQL memory banks. It preserves the producer's
native execution mode: accepted durable work remains asynchronous.

The scope delegates worker admission, shared SQL roles, purpose-specific I/O,
PDF batches, recurring registrations and durable owner lifecycle to the node's
actual executors and counters. Recurring wrappers create no extra coordinator;
closing one scope stops only its own registrations and durable owner IDs.
Receiver addresses remain stable when lease values move. Fallible callbacks
cross independent compilation units through checked named-error dispatch;
PDF callbacks retain the producer's scratch allocation policy. Control and
Raft lease metadata uses the corresponding protected heap.

Native runtime layout ABI 9 rejects earlier lease/handle layouts. Private
storage runtime request ABI 4 validates the old prefix before reading the
execution offer. Storage retains a separate scope until runtime retirement,
child resource-manager destruction, bootstrap header destruction and final
parent credit return have completed. Node teardown waits for these scopes.
The Lite context explicitly passes shared filesystem I/O into file creation
and reopen, avoiding an independently created file executor.

### Funded data-helper runtime ownership (2026-10-18)

DataServer helpers now reuse the stable memory/runtime owner previously used by

shared manager and the backend runtime; metadata's existing module re-exports
that same owner. Eager remote-metadata construction and lazy runtime creation
both apply the configured process limit, inherit a supplied root when present,
and otherwise retain their own root through storage-context and runtime teardown.
The helper root funds both runtime execution and the shared SQL worker bank.
The caller's allocator is preserved, including any limits it imposes.

never destroyed by the helper. This closes the earlier no-parent data-helper

### Cooperative native JSON retention (2026-10-18)

Native retained JSON sizing and ownership now accept the active work control
through a synchronous `Store.JsonLease`. Hashing polls between 4 KiB chunks,
content equality polls between bounded comparisons, and owned byte copies use
cooperative copying. Memo entries are published only after hashing and lookup
succeed, so cancellation cannot leave an uninitialized identity resolution.
The memo still hashes a repeated immutable producer body only once across
sizing retries and retention.

Hash-map comparisons preserve the original cancellation error. The temporary
adapter stops a probe with a provisional match on failure; the caller checks
the captured error before consuming a value or assigning any key/value. Pooled
copy failures release unpublished owners and bytes. These callbacks and their
failure storage never escape the synchronous map operation.

Output pipes use their producer child's execution when one is present. Hash
joins prefer an explicit child execution and otherwise use the coordinator's
statement control. Relation-engine byte polls call the statement checkpoint
without spending a logical row visit per byte chunk. Top-K native retention
receives statement control, including across memo resets. Leased dictionary
imports and scalar append fallbacks also poll their owner. Retained stores,
pooled payloads and published output views do not retain these control pointers.

`native-json-lease-v5` passed 22/22 build steps and 97 selected SQL cases with
no skipped, failed or leaked cases. Coverage includes interrupted hashing before
memo publication and successful retry; forced content-key collisions without
false publication; interrupted pooled copies; actual output-pipe, Top-K and
coordinator hash-join cancellation before retention; native shared bodies and
competitive heap retirement; typed dictionary handoff and allocation faults;
and scoped output views surviving physical producer retirement.

This is the retention part of the main-integration audit. Lazy JSON DOM/cache
materialization, cache-lock waits, frozen decode/encoding, projection cell
access and value-range reads still need consumer-supplied work control and
bounded byte-work verification. No new authority may be retained in a held
output merely to make those paths poll. Transport/global sender bounds,
durable completion/debt admission and the remaining original design requirements
also remain open. Full qualification is still waived.

### Consumer-controlled lazy JSON and projection reads (2026-10-18)

Lazy retained JSON reads now accept the current consumer's `Work.Control`.
`Store.cellControlled`, controlled batch reads and projected/selected readers
forward it synchronously; retained values and caches keep no consumer pointer.
Column pages pass it into native batches and JSON text parsing. Stream column
retention, fallback materialization, delivery projection and sizing use the
current statement's authority. Legacy accessors remain wrappers without control.

Text DOM parsing uses the standard streaming JSON scanner behind a 4 KiB input
reader, with consumer checks before refills and after parsing. Read interruption
restores the original caller error. Parsed strings/number lexemes are owned by
the admitted allocator, independently of the reusable scanner buffer. Frozen
materialization polls recursive nodes and copies leaf bytes cooperatively;
it preserves integer, float and number-string tags.

The lazy-cache physical mutex now protects only constant-time metadata. Decode
runs under an optional token without holding that mutex. Other consumers never
wait for the token: they use their own scratch allocator. The pool token also
serializes encoded-text allocation against cache allocation, while a busy
encoded-text cache declines its optional capability. Publication and rollback
release the token before scratch fallback. Canceled cache attempts release
partial arena/entry charges and leave the cache retryable. Checkpoint callbacks
never run with the physical cache mutex held.

A controlled read preserves an opaque reader's scalar callback and exact row
errors; encoded/frozen representation capabilities cannot substitute for its
validation or policy checks. Adapters can explicitly provide `read_controlled`
when they support the current consumer. This prevents adding cancellation by
silently bypassing existing semantics.
